Couple the first $k$ draws without replacement with $k$ independent uniform position draws: if the independent positions are distinct, keep them; if not, replace them by an independently chosen uniform ordered distinct $k$-tuple. The resulting tuple is uniform among distinct positions and agrees with the original draws except on the collision event. A union bound over the $\binom{k}{2}$ pairs gives collision probability at most $k(k-1)/(2N)$. Hence the type-conditional label marginal differs in total variation from $t^{\otimes k}$ by at most this quantity. Since $t\to p$ in probability and each of the finitely many probabilities $\prod_{r=1}^k t_{i_r}$ is continuous and bounded on the simplex, averaging over shell types proves convergence of the marginal to $p^{\otimes k}$ in total variation.

The rounded shell type and lower bound in step 2.1 give $\liminf_NN^{-1}\log|\Gamma_N|\ge H(p)$. For any shell type $t$, step 1.2 gives the exact identity
$$H(t)=H(p)+\beta\left(\sum_jt_je_j-E\right)-D(t\Vert p)\le H(p)+|\beta|\delta_N/N.$$
There are at most $(N+1)^q$ types, and step 1.1 bounds each multiplicity by $e^{NH(t)}$. Therefore
$$|\Gamma_N|\le(N+1)^q\exp\!\left(NH(p)+|\beta|\delta_N\right).$$
Since $q\log(N+1)/N\to0$ and $\delta_N/N\to0$, the limsup is at most $H(p)$. Together with the lower bound this proves the entropy-density limit, including $\beta=0$, without invoking a nonexistent compactness step.

citations.quote:
Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0},P)$ carry a standard Brownian motion $B$ adapted to the filtration, with future increments independent of the present sigma-algebra. Fix constants $\gamma>0$ and $\sigma>0$, and an $\mathcal F_0$-measurable real random variable $X_0$ with finite second moment. A **continuous adapted solution of the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck equation** on $[0,T]$ is a continuous adapted process $X$ satisfying, almost surely for every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$X_t=X_0-\gamma\int_0^tX_s\,ds+\sigma B_t,$$
where the time integral is the ordinary Lebesgue integral along the continuous path. In differential notation this is $dX_t=-\gamma X_t\,dt+\sigma\,dB_t$, with the stochastic differential interpreted through the displayed integral equation.

The definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. The Itô integral in the explicit representation is the square-integrable predictable-process integral of [[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]].

reviewed.reason: The current F1 now explicitly restricts the solution identity to every t in [0,T] on each finite interval with T>0. This is the source Definition domain, hence contains no negative-time extension. The public theorem already uses nonnegative time.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. A real process
$B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the increments
   $B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}}$ are mutually independent and have laws
   $N(0,t_j-t_{j-1})$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ for every
   $\omega\in A$.

By
[[lem-brownian-gaussian-covariance-is-equivalent-to-independent-stationary-normal-increments]],
the first two clauses are equivalent to saying that $B$ is a centered Gaussian
process with covariance $\min(s,t)$. Clause 3 is additional: it cannot be
recovered from finite-dimensional distributions alone.

No filtration is part of this definition. In particular, no completed or
right-continuous filtration and no Markov or martingale assertion is silently
imposed. Modifications and indistinguishability retain the distinct meanings in
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. The cases
$n=0$, $t_1=0$, and zero-length increments are respectively vacuous or already
covered by $B_0=0$; the increment list itself is strictly increasing.

Choice is declared because the normal-law and Gaussian/increment-equivalence
interfaces construct and identify normal laws under AC. The continuity clause
selects no path and makes no additional use of choice.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. The canonical centered Gaussian coordinate process
with covariance $E[X_sX_t]=\min(s,t)$ has a continuous modification $B$, and
$B$ is a standard Brownian motion. In particular, standard Brownian motion
exists.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]], and fix a probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ with a continuous-time filtration
$(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]] and a standard
Brownian motion $B$ [[def-brownian-motion]] on it. **Standing hypothesis
(H).** $B$ is adapted to $(\mathcal F_t)$ and for all $0\le s<t$ the increment
$B_t-B_s$ is independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and has law $N(0,t-s)$. The raw
natural filtration and the usual augmented natural filtration
[[def-natural-and-usual-augmented-brownian-filtrations]] both satisfy (H) for a
standard Brownian motion, by
[[thm-brownian-future-path-markov-property]]; for a general filtration, (H) is
part of the data and is not automatic. Every statement in this development
names (H) when it is used.

Throughout, fix a finite horizon $T>0$. An **elementary predictable Brownian
integrand** on $[0,T]$ is a process of the form
$$H_s(\omega)=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\xi_k(\omega)\,1_{(t_k,t_{k+1}]}(s),\qquad s\in[0,T],$$
where $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_m=T$ is a finite partition of $[0,T]$, each
$\xi_k$ is a bounded real $\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable random variable, and
the values at the partition points are irrelevant because the intervals are
left-open and right-closed. The **mesh** of the representation is
$\max_k(t_{k+1}-t_k)$, and the **supremum norm** of the representation is
$\max_k\|\xi_k\|_\infty$. The integrand itself is the process $H$; a second
list of the same name with different coefficients is the same elementary
integrand only if the two processes coincide in the almost-everywhere sense
made precise below.

The following properties are part of the definition and are used at once.

1. **Predictability.** $H$ is predictable
   [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]. Indeed, for a
   Borel set $\Gamma\subseteq\mathbb R$,
   $$\{H\in\Gamma\}=Z_\Gamma\cup\bigcup_{k=0}^{m-1}\bigl((t_k,t_{k+1}]\times\{\xi_k\in\Gamma\}\bigr), \qquad Z_\Gamma:=\begin{cases}\{0\}\times\Omega,&0\in\Gamma,\\\varnothing,&0\notin\Gamma,\end{cases}$$
   a finite union of generators of the predictable sigma-algebra because
   $\{\xi_k\in\Gamma\}\in\mathcal F_{t_k}$ and
   $\{0\}\times\Omega$ is a time-zero generator. Consequently $H$ is progressively
   measurable and measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,T])\otimes\mathcal F$, and $H$ belongs to
   $L^2([0,T]\times\Omega,\mathrm dt\otimes P)$: with
   $c:=\max_k\|\xi_k\|_\infty<\infty$ one has
   $E\int_0^TH_s^2\,ds\le c^2T<\infty$.

2. **Endpoint and null-set conventions.** Replacing the intervals by
   $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$ makes the value at $s=0$ zero for every elementary
   integrand. More generally, if two elementary integrands agree for all
   $s\in[0,T]$ except at finitely many deterministic times, then they agree
   $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-almost everywhere, since a finite set of times is
   Lebesgue-null and Tonelli computes
   $\mathrm dt\otimes P(\{u\}\times\Omega)=0$. All integrands and all
   integrals below are therefore elements of the quotient spaces of
   $L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$ and $L^2(P)$; a claim about a process is a claim
   about its almost-everywhere class unless a representative is explicitly
   named, and path statements name the continuous representative.

3. **Deterministic coefficients.** If every $\xi_k$ is a deterministic real
   number, $H$ is a deterministic step function on $[0,T]$, so the elementary
   integrands include all step functions with deterministic coefficients. These
   are the integrands for which the integral is a Gaussian variable below.

The Axiom of Choice is declared because the Brownian construction and the
conditional-expectation interface used in items 6, 7 and 13 assume it; the
definition itself, including the predictability computation of clause 1, uses
no choice. The countable-choice obligations inherited from that interface are declared
as dependencies of this item.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix a horizon $T>0$ and let
$\mathcal P_T$ be the predictable sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$
[[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]. Let $H$ be a
predictable process with
$$E\int_0^TH_s^2\,ds=\int_{[0,T]\times\Omega}H^2\,d(\mathrm dt\otimes P)<\infty ,$$
so that $H$ is an element of the quotient space
$L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$ over $\mathcal P_T$; its class is what is integrated.
The **Ito integral** $\int_0^TH_s\,dB_s$, also written $H\cdot B$ or $I_T(H)$,
is defined as follows.

1. **Construction.** By the density theorem
   [[thm-density-of-elementary-predictable-processes-in-predictable-l2]] there
   is a sequence $(H^n)$ of bounded elementary predictable integrands
   [[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]] with
   $\|H^n-H\|_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)}\to0$. For such a sequence the
   elementary integrals $I_T(H^n)$
   [[def-ito-integral-of-an-elementary-predictable-process]] form a Cauchy
   sequence in $L^2(P)$: by the elementary isometry
   [[thm-ito-isometry-for-elementary-integrands]] and the well-definedness of
   the elementary integral,
   $$E\bigl(I_T(H^n)-I_T(H^m)\bigr)^2=E\int_0^T(H^n-H^m)^2ds=\|H^n-H^m\|^2_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)} ,$$
   and the right-hand side tends to $0$. Since $L^2(P)$ is complete
   [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]], the classes $I_T(H^n)$ converge
   in $L^2(P)$; the limit is a class in $L^2(P)$, and
   $$\int_0^TH_s\,dB_s:=\lim_{n\to\infty}I_T(H^n)\qquad\text{in }L^2(P).$$
   The limit is a random variable only up to almost-sure equality; statements
   about it are statements about that class. The limit does not depend on the
   chosen sequence: if another elementary sequence $K^n\to H$ is used, then
   the elementary isometry and linearity give
   $$\|I_T(H^n)-I_T(K^n)\|_{L^2(P)} =\|H^n-K^n\|_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)} \le\|H^n-H\|_2+\|K^n-H\|_2\longrightarrow0,$$
   so the two $L^2(P)$ limits agree.

2. **Integrals at a time.** For $t\in[0,T]$ put
   $\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s:=\int_0^TH_s1_{[0,t]}(s)\,dB_s$, the construction of
   clause 1 applied to the truncated process $H1_{[0,t]}$. That process is
   predictable: $H$ is $\mathcal P_T$-measurable and $1_{[0,t]}$ is a
   deterministic predictable indicator, so the product is
   $\mathcal P_T$-measurable; and it is square-integrable because
   $|H1_{[0,t]}|\le|H|$ pointwise. The same construction applied to $H$
   itself gives $t=T$. The family
   $\bigl(\int_0^tH\,dB\bigr)_{t\in[0,T]}$ is a family of $L^2(P)$-classes
   indexed by $t$; its continuous version is supplied by item 13, and no path
   property is asserted by this definition.

3. **Consistency with elementary integrands.** If $H$ is itself elementary,
   then the constant sequence $H^n:=H$ is admissible in clause 1, so
   $\int_0^TH\,dB$ is the limit of the constant sequence of elementary sums,
   namely the elementary sum $I_T(H)$ of
   [[def-ito-integral-of-an-elementary-predictable-process]]. The same argument
   with $H1_{[0,t]}$ in place of $H$, and the finite telescoping of the
   elementary sum over a refinement containing $t$, gives
   $\int_0^tH\,dB=I_t(H)$ for every $t\in[0,T]$. In particular the general
   definition extends, rather than replaces, the elementary definition.

4. **Linearity in the integrand is not asserted here.** Clause 1 defines each
   integral separately from an arbitrary approximating sequence; the linear and
   isometric properties of the extension are item 12. Until item 12 is proved,
   linearity may be used only for elementary integrands, where it is part of
   [[def-ito-integral-of-an-elementary-predictable-process]].

5. **Comparison with deterministic Riemann integration.** The integral is a
   stochastic integral: the integrand is paired with the Brownian path through
   left-endpoint sums and an $L^2(P)$ limit. This definition does not assert
   convergence of arbitrary tagged Riemann--Stieltjes sums for a general
   predictable integrand. Particular integrands can have a pathwise
   interpretation: for $H\equiv1$ every tagged sum telescopes to $B_T-B_0$,
   which is also its Ito integral by clause 3 (the value at time zero is
   irrelevant to its product-measure class). The notation $\int_0^TH\,dB$
   here always refers to the $L^2(P)$-class defined above.

The Axiom of Choice is declared because the construction selects an
approximating sequence and uses the completeness and conditional-expectation
interfaces that assume it; the inherited obligations are declared as
dependencies of this item. An alternative construction that avoids selecting the sequence is
not needed, because clause 1 shows every sequence gives the same class.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix $T>0$. For predictable
$H,K$ with finite energy $E\int_0^TH^2ds,E\int_0^TK^2ds<\infty$ the integrals
$\int_0^TH\,dB$ of
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] satisfy
$$\int_0^T(H+K)\,dB=\int_0^TH\,dB+\int_0^TK\,dB,\qquad \int_0^T(aH)\,dB=a\int_0^TH\,dB\quad(a\in\mathbb R),$$
and the identities are equalities of $L^2(P)$-classes (almost sure
equalities). Moreover the map $H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is an isometry,
$$E\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)^2=E\int_0^TH^2ds=\|H\|^2_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)},$$
it takes values in the mean-zero subspace of $L^2(P)$, and the bilinear cross
identity
$$E\Bigl[\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)\Bigl(\int_0^TK\,dB\Bigr)\Bigr]=E\int_0^TH_sK_s\,ds$$
holds for all such $H,K$. In particular the image of the map is a closed
subspace of $L^2(P)$ isometric to the predictable $L^2$ space of $H$'s, and
$H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is injective up to the $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-class.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $H$ be a predictable
process with $E\int_0^TH_s^2ds<\infty$ for every finite $T$. Then there is an
adapted process $M=(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ with continuous paths such that
$M_t=\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s$ almost surely for every $t\ge0$
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]], and $M$ is a
square-integrable martingale relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$
[[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]]: $EM_t^2=E\int_0^tH_s^2ds<\infty$
for every $t$. Any two such continuous versions agree at every time on one
measurable event of probability one; in particular the continuous version is
unique in this common-full-measure-event sense, and it is the only continuous
square-integrable martingale whose value at each deterministic $t$ is the
integral class.

This conclusion is deliberately distinguished from the exact definition of
indistinguishability in
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. On a
noncomplete probability space the full equality set, although it contains the
measurable probability-one event constructed below, need not itself be
measurable. On a complete probability space the two notions coincide, because
the complement of the equality set is then a measurable subset of a null set.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix $T>0$ and let
$h\in L^2[0,T]$ be deterministic, choose a Borel representative of its
Lebesgue-equivalence class, and set $h(s,\omega):=h(s)$. This process is
predictable with finite energy. Then the Ito integral
$\int_0^Th_s\,dB_s$
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] is centered
normal with variance $\int_0^Th^2ds$: its law is $N(0,\int_0^Th^2ds)$ in the
convention of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]], where $N(0,0)$ is the
Dirac law at $0$. More generally, for deterministic $h_1,\dots,h_d\in L^2[0,T]$
the vector of integrals is jointly Gaussian in the sense of
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]]: its law is $N_d(0,\Sigma)$ with
$$\Sigma_{jk}=\int_0^Th_j(s)h_k(s)\,ds .$$
In particular the covariance of the pair is
$\operatorname{Cov}(\int h_jdB,\int h_kdB)=\int h_jh_k$, the integrals are
uncorrelated exactly when $\int h_jh_k=0$, and integrals of deterministic
integrands with disjoint supports are independent.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathcal H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $A$ be self-adjoint with regular Borel projection-valued measure $E$ from [[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], with $E((-\infty,a))=0$ for finite $a\in\mathbb R$. For each $\gamma>0$, define the bounded Gibbs operator $K_\gamma:=\Phi_E(f_\gamma)$ using the bounded Borel PVM integral of [[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]], where $f_\gamma(\lambda)=e^{-\gamma\lambda}$ for $\lambda\ge a$ and $f_\gamma(\lambda)=e^{-\gamma a}$ for $\lambda<a$. Fix $\beta>0$ and suppose $K_\beta$ is trace class in the sense of [[def-trace-class-operator]]. Then $K_\beta$ is injective and has a finite or countable orthonormal basis $(u_j)$ of $\mathcal H$ with $Au_j=E_ju_j$, $E_j\ge a$, and $K_\beta u_j=e^{-\beta E_j}u_j$. Its partition function $Z_\beta:=\operatorname{Tr}K_\beta=\sum_j e^{-\beta E_j}$ is positive and finite, and $\rho_\beta:=K_\beta/Z_\beta$ is positive with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho_\beta=1$. For every $B\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\beta B)=\sum_j(e^{-\beta E_j}/Z_\beta)\langle Bu_j,u_j\rangle$ absolutely. Further, let $J\subset(0,\infty)$ be open and suppose that for every compact $C\subset J$ there is a summable family $a_j\ge0$ with $(1+|E_j|^2)e^{-\gamma E_j}\le a_j$ for all $j$ and $\gamma\in C$. Then for each $\gamma\in J$, $K_\gamma$ is trace class with partition function $Z_\gamma:=\operatorname{Tr}K_\gamma=\sum_j e^{-\gamma E_j}$. With $p_j(\gamma):=e^{-\gamma E_j}/Z_\gamma$, define $\bar E_\gamma:=\sum_jp_j(\gamma)E_j$, $\operatorname{Var}_\gamma(E):=\sum_jp_j(\gamma)(E_j-\bar E_\gamma)^2$, and $S_\gamma:=-\sum_jp_j(\gamma)\log p_j(\gamma)$. These quantities are finite and satisfy $-\partial_\gamma\log Z_\gamma=\bar E_\gamma$, $\partial_\gamma^2\log Z_\gamma=\operatorname{Var}_\gamma(E)$, and $S_\gamma=\log Z_\gamma+\gamma\bar E_\gamma$ as in [[thm-tdmath-summable-canonical-differentiation]]. Countable nonnegative sums use the finite-subsum supremum convention of [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$, $K$
and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. the trace-class operators $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]])
   form a linear subspace of $\mathcal B(H,K)$ on which $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm,
   and
   $$\|T\|\le\|T\|_1\qquad\text{for every }T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$$
   ([[def-operator-norm]]);
2. if $T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ and $A\in\mathcal B(K,L)$, $B\in\mathcal B(H_0,H)$
   are bounded linear operators on Hilbert spaces $H_0,L$, then
   $ATB\in\mathcal S_1(H_0,L)$ and
   $$\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\| ;$$
3. $(\mathcal S_1(H,K),\|\cdot\|_1)$ is a Banach space: every
   $\|\cdot\|_1$-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ has a limit in
   $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ to which it converges in $\|\cdot\|_1$
   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],
   [[def-metric-space]]).

Assume Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a separable complex Hilbert space, let
$T\in\mathcal S_1(H)$ be trace class, and let $(P_n)_{n\ge1}$ be any supplied sequence of
finite-rank orthogonal projections on $H$ such that $P_n\to I$ strongly. Then
$$\|P_nTP_n-T\|_1\longrightarrow0.$$
The projections need not be increasing. For example, the initial projections
onto the first $n$ vectors of a supplied countable orthonormal basis satisfy
the hypothesis.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a **self-adjoint positive** trace-class operator
([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-trace-class-operator]]), so that $\langle Tx,x\rangle\ge0$ for every
$x\in H$. Let $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots>0$ be the positive eigenvalues of
$T$ listed with multiplicity
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]) and let
$(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$ be the zero-padded singular-value sequence
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]). Then
$s_n(T)=\lambda_n$ for every $n$, and
$$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n=\|T\|_1 ,$$
where the sum is over the positive eigenvalues with multiplicity and the
equalities are also valid in the finite-rank case (then $\lambda_n:=0$ for
$n$ beyond the rank). This is the positive compact self-adjoint case only; it is
**not** Lidskii's theorem for arbitrary trace-class operators, which is not
claimed here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then:

1. for every **nuclear representation** $Tx=\sum_j\langle x,u_j\rangle v_j$ of
   $T$ (operator-norm convergence of the partial sums,
   $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<+\infty$), the scalar series $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$
   converges absolutely and
   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$
2. the sum $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$ depends only on $T$; denoting it
   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   without assuming that $H$ has a Hilbert basis;
3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);
4. the trace is linear in the trace-class variable and bounded by the trace
   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,
   $\operatorname{tr}(aS+bT)=a\operatorname{tr}(S)+b\operatorname{tr}(T)$ and
   $|\operatorname{tr}(T)|\le\|T\|_1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]) and let
$S\in\mathcal B(H)$ be bounded. Then $ST$ and $TS$ are trace class and
$$\operatorname{tr}(ST)=\operatorname{tr}(TS) .$$
If $A,B\in\mathcal B(H)$ are Hilbert–Schmidt relative to a supplied Hilbert
basis $E$ of $H$ ([[def-hilbert-schmidt-operator]]), then the products $AB$ and
$BA$ are trace class and
$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

derivations.claim: Each multiplier $e^{-iE_jt/\hbar}$ has modulus one by [F6]. Thus $U_t$ preserves the norm of finite linear combinations of the complete orthonormal basis; it extends by density to an isometry on the Hilbert space. The similarly defined $U_{-t}$ is its inverse, so $U_t$ is unitary and depends continuously on $t$ on each finite-dimensional energy span. The arguments $E_jt/\hbar$ are dimensionless.

By [F2], $\rho_t=U_t\rho U_t^*$ is trace class. It is positive because $\langle\rho_t x,x\rangle=\langle\rho U_t^*x,U_t^*x\rangle\ge0$, and cyclicity [F5] gives $\operatorname{Tr}\rho_t=\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$.

Enumerate the distinct energy eigenspaces and let $P_N$ project onto the first $N$ of them, with $P_N=I$ after the list is exhausted if it is finite. Their union spans the eigenbasis, so $P_N\to I$ strongly. The Hilbert space is separable by the countable complete basis in [A1]. Therefore [F3] gives $\|P_N\rho P_N-\rho\|_1\to0$. Unitary invariance of trace norm follows from [F2] in both directions: $\|U_tRU_t^*\|_1\le\|R\|_1$ and $R=U_t^*(U_tRU_t^*)U_t$ gives the reverse inequality. Consequently $$\|U_tP_N\rho P_NU_t^*-\rho_t\|_1=\|P_N\rho P_N-\rho\|_1$$ uniformly in $t$.

For fixed $N$, the matrix of $U_tP_N\rho P_NU_t^*$ on its finite-dimensional range has continuous entries, hence is continuous in trace norm. Step 2.2 makes $\rho_t$ a uniform trace-norm limit on compact time intervals of these continuous maps; therefore $t\mapsto\rho_t$ is trace-norm continuous. On $[0,T]$ it is uniformly continuous. Riemann sums for a uniformly continuous Banach-valued function are Cauchy: two sums are compared on a common refinement and their difference is bounded by $T$ times the modulus of continuity at the larger mesh. Completeness in [F2] supplies the trace-class integral and its usual norm bound.

In the eigenbasis, the $(i,j)$ matrix entry of $U_tP_N\rho P_NU_t^*$ is $\langle\rho u_j,u_i\rangle e^{i(E_j-E_i)t/\hbar}$. Its time-average factor is $1$ if $E_i=E_j$; if $E_i\ne E_j$, direct integration using [F6] gives absolute value at most $2\hbar/(T|E_j-E_i|)$, which tends to zero. Since the compression is finite dimensional, entrywise convergence implies trace-norm convergence. Hence the finite compressed average tends to $\sum_{E\text{ among the first }N}P_E\rho P_E$.

Each block $P_E\rho P_E$ is positive trace class. The sum of their traces is $$\sum_E\sum_{u_j\in\operatorname{ran}P_E}\langle\rho u_j,u_j\rangle =\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$$ by [F4] and the complete basis in [A1]. Therefore their finite partial sums are Cauchy in trace norm: for a positive finite block tail its trace norm equals its trace, and the scalar trace tail tends to zero. Their limit $\rho_{\rm diag}$ exists in trace norm, is positive, and has trace one.

Given $\epsilon>0$, choose $N$ so the compression error in step 2.2 and the diagonal tail in step 5.1 are each below $\epsilon/3$. The norm bound for the Riemann integral in step 3.1 makes the average of the compression error at most $\epsilon/3$, uniformly in $T$. For this fixed $N$, step 4.1 makes the finite compressed average differ from its finite diagonal limit by less than $\epsilon/3$ for all sufficiently large $T$. The triangle inequality then gives $\|\bar\rho_T-\rho_{\rm diag}\|_1<\epsilon$.

For bounded observable $B$, the trace-class ideal and trace estimates in [F2] and [F4] give $|\operatorname{Tr}((\bar\rho_T-\rho_{\rm diag})B)|\le\|\bar\rho_T-\rho_{\rm diag}\|_1\|B\|$. Step 6.1 sends the right-hand side to zero. The conclusion is only convergence of time-averaged states in the stated trace norm.

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

derivations.claim: The unitary evolution sends $\psi$ to $(e^{-iE_1t/\hbar}u_1+e^{-iE_2t/\hbar}u_2)/\sqrt2$, which remains a unit vector by [F2]. Its rank-one density has eigenvalues $1,0$, so its entropy is $-k_B(1\log1+0\log0)=0$ for every $t$.

The two energy eigenspaces are one-dimensional. The matrix entry between them is an exponential with nonzero frequency; by [F1] its average has magnitude at most $\hbar/(T|E_1-E_2|)$ and tends to zero. The diagonal entries remain $1/2$, so the direct finite-dimensional average yields $\rho_{\rm diag}=\tfrac12P_1+\tfrac12P_2$. Its eigenvalues are $(1/2,1/2)$, so $$S(\rho_{\rm diag})=-k_B\left(\tfrac12\log\tfrac12+\tfrac12\log\tfrac12\right)=k_B\log2.$$ Since every $S(\rho_t)=0$, the time average of instantaneous entropy is exactly zero.

In the basis $(u_1,u_2)$, $\bar\rho_T$ has diagonal entries $1/2$ and off-diagonal entry $$c_T=\frac1{2T}\int_0^T e^{-i(E_1-E_2)t/\hbar}\,dt,$$ whose magnitude is at most $\hbar/(T|E_1-E_2|)$ by direct integration. Its eigenvalues are $1/2\pm|c_T|$, so both tend to $1/2$. Continuity of $x\mapsto-x\log x$ at $1/2$ gives $S(\bar\rho_T)\to k_B\log2$. Thus entropy of the averaged state has a nonzero limit even though the averaged instantaneous entropy remains zero.

citations.quote:
$F$ is a **complete ordered field** (equivalently, $F$ has the
**least-upper-bound property**, or is **Dedekind complete**) if every nonempty
$S \subseteq F$ that is bounded above has a least upper bound in $F$.

The set of **natural numbers** is the **smallest inductive set**
([[def-inductive-set]]),

$$\mathbb{N} = \omega := \bigcap\,\{\, I : I \text{ is inductive} \,\},$$

which exists and is itself inductive by [[lem-omega-smallest-inductive]] (the
Axiom of Infinity, [[def-axiom-of-infinity]], supplies one inductive set to
intersect within, and Separation, [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]], makes the
intersection a set). On $\mathbb{N}$ we take

$$0 := \varnothing, \qquad \sigma(n) := n \cup \{n\},$$

the distinguished element and the successor function. Thus
$0 = \varnothing$, $1 = \{0\}$, $2 = \{0, 1\}$, $3 = \{0, 1, 2\}$, and in general
$n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ is the set of its predecessors.

**Addition** $+ : \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is defined by
recursion on the second argument: for each fixed $m \in \mathbb{N}$,

$$m + 0 = m, \qquad m + \sigma(n) = \sigma(m + n).$$
For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$: $m + n = n + m$.
For all $n \in \mathbb{N}$: $0 + n = n$. The right identity $n + 0 = n$ is definitional, so together with this law $0$ is a two-sided identity for addition.

For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, define the **order** by

$$m \le n \iff \exists k \in \mathbb{N}\ (m + k = n),$$

and the **strict order** by $m < n \iff (m \le n \text{ and } m \neq n)$, using
addition ([[def-nat-addition]]).

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]) with additive identity $0_F$ and
multiplicative identity $1_F$. Define
$\iota : \mathbb{N} \to F$ by recursion on $\mathbb{N}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[thm-recursion]]):

$$\iota(0) \;:=\; 0_F, \qquad \iota(n+1) \;:=\; \iota(n) + 1_F .$$

$\iota(n)$ is the **canonical natural** of $n$ in $F$. It is also written
$n \cdot 1_F$, and for $n \ge 1$ it is $1_F$ added to itself $n$ times.

**Why the notation is needed at all.** A natural number in this library is a von
Neumann natural, that is a set ([[def-natural-numbers]]), and a set is not an
element of $F$. So $1/n$, $n^{\alpha}$ and $x/n$ are not expressions of $F$ when
$n$ is a natural: what they mean is $1/\iota(n)$, $\iota(n)^{\alpha}$ and
$x/\iota(n)$. The map $\iota$ is what carries a counting number into the field,
and writing it is the whole reason a reader meets $1/\iota(k+1)$ where an
informal text would write $1/(k+1)$.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]) with additive identity $0_F$ and
multiplicative identity $1_F$. Define
$\iota : \mathbb{N} \to F$ by recursion on $\mathbb{N}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[thm-recursion]]):

$$\iota(0) \;:=\; 0_F, \qquad \iota(n+1) \;:=\; \iota(n) + 1_F .$$

$\iota(n)$ is the **canonical natural** of $n$ in $F$. It is also written
$n \cdot 1_F$, and for $n \ge 1$ it is $1_F$ added to itself $n$ times.

**Why the notation is needed at all.** A natural number in this library is a von
Neumann natural, that is a set ([[def-natural-numbers]]), and a set is not an
element of $F$. So $1/n$, $n^{\alpha}$ and $x/n$ are not expressions of $F$ when
$n$ is a natural: what they mean is $1/\iota(n)$, $\iota(n)^{\alpha}$ and
$x/\iota(n)$. The map $\iota$ is what carries a counting number into the field,
and writing it is the whole reason a reader meets $1/\iota(k+1)$ where an
informal text would write $1/(k+1)$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field, with field structure as in [[def-field]], and for
$n \ge 1$ let $n \cdot 1_F$ denote the canonical natural number
$\underbrace{1_F + \cdots + 1_F}_{n}$, defined recursively by $1 \cdot 1_F = 1_F$
and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F = n \cdot 1_F + 1_F$. Then for every $n \ge 1$:

- $n \cdot 1_F > 0$ and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F > n \cdot 1_F$;
- the map $n \mapsto n \cdot 1_F$ is strictly increasing, hence injective, on $\{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$;
- $(m+n) \cdot 1_F = m \cdot 1_F + n \cdot 1_F$ and $(mn) \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F)$ for all $m, n \ge 1$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]). There is a unique field
homomorphism $\iota : \mathbb{Q} \to F$ ([[def-field-homomorphism]]). On the
integers it is given by $n \mapsto n \cdot 1_F$ (with $-n \mapsto -(n \cdot 1_F)$
and $0 \mapsto 0$), and on a rational written as $p/q$ with $q \ge 1$ by
$\iota(p/q) = \iota(p)\,(q \cdot 1_F)^{-1}$. Moreover $\iota$ is injective and
order-preserving, so it is an embedding of $\mathbb{Q}$ as an ordered subfield of
$F$, and it is the only field homomorphism $\mathbb{Q} \to F$.

In any ordered field $F$ with positive cone $P$, the multiplicative identity
satisfies $0 < 1$; that is, $1 \in P$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ then $a^{-1} > 0$.
2. If $0 < a < b$ then $0 < b^{-1} < a^{-1}$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b, c \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ and $b > 0$ then $ab > 0$.
2. If $a > 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab < 0$.
3. If $a < 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab > 0$.
4. If $c > 0$ then $a < b \iff ac < bc$.
5. If $c < 0$ then $a < b \iff bc < ac$ (multiplication by a negative reverses order).

A sequence $(x_k)$ of reals **converges** to $x \in \mathbb{R}$ when for
every rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $K$ with
$|x_k - x| < \hat\varepsilon$ for all $k \ge K$. It is **Cauchy** when for
every rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $K$ with
$|x_k - x_l| < \hat\varepsilon$ for all $k, l \ge K$.

derivations.claim: The set $N_{\mathbb R}:=\{\iota_{\mathbb N}(n):n\in\mathbb N\}$ is nonempty. If it were bounded above, completeness [F1] would give $s=\sup N_{\mathbb R}$. Since $1>0$ by [F4], $s-1<s$, so $s-1$ is not an upper bound; choose $n\in\mathbb N$ with $\iota_{\mathbb N}(n)>s-1$. By the successor rule in [F3], $\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(n))=\iota_{\mathbb N}(n)+1>s$, while $\sigma(n)\in\mathbb N$, contradicting that $s$ is an upper bound. Hence $N_{\mathbb R}$ is unbounded above.

For every $n\in\mathbb N$, $\sigma(n)=1+n$ by natural-addition commutativity and the successor rule, so $1\le\sigma(n)$ by the definition of natural order; hence $\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(n))>0$ by [F3]. The successor recursion gives $\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(\sigma(n)))=\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(n))+1>\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(n))$, since $1>0$. Reciprocation reverses this strict inequality by [F4], hence $0<\epsilon_n$ and $\epsilon_{n+1}<\epsilon_n$. Now fix rational $q>0$ and let $\hat q>0$ be its real image. By step 1.1 choose $N\in\mathbb N$ with $\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(N))>1/\hat q$. If $n\ge N$, then $\sigma(N)\le\sigma(n)$ by [F2] and [[lem-nat-order-add-compatible]], and the increasing-map clause of [F3] gives $\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(n))\ge\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(N))$. Therefore $0<\epsilon_n\le 1/\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(N))<\hat q$. This is convergence to zero by [F5].

boundaries.reason: In the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$, the sequence $\epsilon_n:=1/(n+1)$, $n\in\mathbb N$, is positive, strictly decreasing, and converges to zero. Boundary empty: No empty family is quantified in the Statement; the input domain is fixed there.

Fix a nonempty set $X$ and the compounds of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. A **comparison relation** $\preceq$ is defined only for pairs $(A,B)$ with $m(A)=m(B)$. Write $A\sim B$ when both $A\preceq B$ and $B\preceq A$; this is equivalence, not equality of coefficient functions. The following are explicit hypotheses on $\preceq$:

1. **Preorder:** $A\preceq A$, and $A\preceq B\preceq C$ implies $A\preceq C$.
2. **Composition consistency:** $A\preceq B$ implies $A+C\preceq B+C$ for every compound $C$.
3. **Positive scaling:** $A\preceq B$ implies $tA\preceq tB$ for every real $t>0$.
4. **Splitting and recombination:** for $x\in X$, $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, the one-state compound $te_x$ is equivalent to $se_x+(t-s)e_x$.
5. **Stability:** for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive compounds $Z_0,Z_1$ with $m(Z_0)=m(Z_1)$, and a sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to $0$, if $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\preceq B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for every $n$, then $A\preceq B$.
6. **Comparison hypothesis (CH):** for every equal-mass pair $A,B$, either $A\preceq B$ or $B\preceq A$ (or both).

These are mathematical assumptions, not conclusions about a physical system. No antisymmetry, continuity, convexity, or strict comparison is included. Strict comparison means $A\preceq B$ and not $B\preceq A$.

Let $X$ be a set of state labels. A **tagged scalable compound over $X$** is a function $c:X\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$ whose support $\operatorname{supp}(c):=\{x\in X:c(x)\ne0\}$ is finite. The coefficient is a dimensionless formal amount; state labels retain their tags, so equal coefficients on different labels do not identify those labels. Compounds are equal exactly when their coefficient functions are equal.

For compounds $c,d$ and $t\ge0$, define composition and nonnegative scaling pointwise by $(c+d)(x):=c(x)+d(x)$ and $(tc)(x):=t c(x)$. The zero function is the empty compound; in particular $0c=0$. Comparison axioms involving scaling still require a strictly positive scalar unless explicitly stated otherwise. The **mass** of $c$ is the finite sum $m(c):=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}c(x)$. It is dimensionless bookkeeping mass, not thermodynamic mass or energy. The compound is positive when $m(c)>0$.

For every state label $x\in X$, the **unit-state compound** $e_x$ is the coefficient function with $e_x(y)=1$ if $y=x$ and $e_x(y)=0$ otherwise. Its support is $\{x\}$, so it is a tagged compound. In compound comparisons, a state label $x$ denotes $e_x$. Every compound has the canonical finite decomposition $c=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}c(x)e_x$, with an empty sum when $c=0$; coefficients on this support are strictly positive. The mass-one property $m(e_x)=1$ and the equivalence $m(c)=0\Longleftrightarrow c=0$ are proved in [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

The formula for mass is independent of the chosen finite set containing the support, and composition and scaling obey $m(c+d)=m(c)+m(d)$ and $m(tc)=t m(c)$; [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]] proves these assertions.

For every tagged scalable compound $c$, the mass in [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] is independent of the finite summation set used. For any compounds $c,d$ and $t\ge0$, $m(c+d)=m(c)+m(d)$ and $m(tc)=t m(c)$; $m(0)=0$. For every $x\in X$, the unit-state compound $e_x$ has $m(e_x)=1$. A compound has zero mass if and only if it is the empty compound.

Let $u,v:X\to\mathbb R$ be finite-support real coefficient maps with equal total coefficient $\sum_xu(x)=\sum_xv(x)$. These signed maps are formal comparison notation, not compounds. Put $d:=v-u$ and define $d^+(x):=\max\{d(x),0\}$ and $d^-(x):=\max\{-d(x),0\}$. Then $d^+,d^-$ are nonnegative finite-support compounds of equal mass, as verified in [[lem-tdmath-spectator-cancellation]]. Define

$$u\preceq_s v\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d^-\preceq d^+,$$

using the compound comparison relation of [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]]. Thus positive coefficients of $v-u$ remain on the right and negative coefficients move to the left. Signed notation is never a claim that a negative amount of a physical system exists.

Under [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]], for equal-mass compounds $A,B,C$, $A+C\preceq B+C$ if and only if $A\preceq B$. The signed relation of [[def-tdmath-signed-comparison]] is well-defined; on nonnegative equal-mass maps it agrees with $\preceq$, is invariant under adding the same finite-support signed map to both sides, and is transitive and closed under adding two comparisons.

Then $d^+,d^-$ are nonnegative finite-support compounds of equal mass, as verified in [[lem-tdmath-spectator-cancellation]]. Define

$$u\preceq_s v\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d^-\preceq d^+,$$

using the compound comparison relation of [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]]. Thus positive coefficients of $v-u$ remain on the right and negative coefficients move to the left. Signed notation is never a claim that a negative amount of a physical system exists.

Let $x_0,x_1\in X$ satisfy $x_0\preceq x_1$ and not $x_1\preceq x_0$. For every real $\lambda$, define the signed unit-mass reference map $R_\lambda:=(1-\lambda)e_{x_0}+\lambda e_{x_1}$. For all $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb R$,

$$R_\lambda\preceq_s R_\mu\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\lambda\le\mu.$$

The parameters need not lie in $[0,1]$; outside that interval $R_\lambda$ is signed notation, not a compound.
In the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$, the sequence $\epsilon_n:=1/(n+1)$, $n\in\mathbb N$, is positive, strictly decreasing, and converges to zero.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and $S \subseteq F$.

- $u \in F$ is an **upper bound** of $S$ if $s \le u$ for all $s \in S$; $S$ is
  **bounded above** if it has an upper bound.
- $u \in F$ is a **least upper bound** (or **supremum**, $\sup S$) of $S$ if $u$
  is an upper bound of $S$ and $u \le u'$ for every upper bound $u'$ of $S$.

$F$ is a **complete ordered field** (equivalently, $F$ has the
**least-upper-bound property**, or is **Dedekind complete**) if every nonempty
$S \subseteq F$ that is bounded above has a least upper bound in $F$.

derivations.claim: Write $q_n:=\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(n))>0$, so $\epsilon_n=1/q_n$ by [F4]. Suppose no $n\in\mathbb N$ satisfies $(q_n+1)e_{x_0}\preceq q_ne_{x_1}+e_x$. Both sides have mass $q_n+1$, so CH gives $q_ne_{x_1}+e_x\preceq(q_n+1)e_{x_0}$. Scale by $1/q_n=\epsilon_n$ to obtain $e_{x_1}+\epsilon_ne_x\preceq e_{x_0}+\epsilon_ne_{x_0}$. Apply stability to the sequence $\epsilon_n$, with bases $e_{x_1},e_{x_0}$ and positive unit-mass spectators $e_x,e_{x_0}$. It yields $x_1\preceq x_0$, contradicting strictness. Thus some $n$ has $(q_n+1)e_{x_0}\preceq q_ne_{x_1}+e_x$, which by signed translation and cancellation in [F2] is $R_{-q_n}\preceq_s e_x$; hence $-q_n\in L_x$.

Suppose $L_x$ is unbounded above. For each $n\in\mathbb N$, unboundedness supplies $\lambda\in L_x$ with $\lambda>q_n$; [F3] gives $R_{q_n}\preceq_sR_\lambda$, and transitivity gives $q_n\in L_x$. Since $q_n\ge1$ by [F4], adding the common compound $q_ne_{x_0}$ to $R_{q_n}$ and $e_x$ makes them $e_{x_0}+q_ne_{x_1}$ and $e_x+q_ne_{x_0}$. Thus [F2] identifies $R_{q_n}\preceq_s e_x$ with the compound comparison between those maps. Scaling by $\epsilon_n=1/q_n$ gives $e_{x_1}+\epsilon_ne_{x_0}\preceq e_{x_0}+\epsilon_ne_x$. Stability with bases $e_{x_1},e_{x_0}$ and positive unit-mass spectators $e_{x_0},e_x$ now yields $x_1\preceq x_0$, again a contradiction. Therefore $L_x$ is bounded above.

If $\lambda\in L_x$ and $\mu\le\lambda$, [F3] gives $R_\mu\preceq_sR_\lambda$; signed transitivity and $R_\lambda\preceq_s e_x$ imply $\mu\in L_x$. Thus $L_x$ is downward closed. By steps 1.1 and 1.2 it is nonempty and bounded above, so [F5] supplies the real number $s:=\sup L_x$.

For each $n\in\mathbb N$, $s-\epsilon_n$ is not an upper bound of $L_x$, so some $\lambda\in L_x$ has $\lambda>s-\epsilon_n$. Downward closure gives $s-\epsilon_n\in L_x$. Consistency then gives $R_s+\epsilon_ne_{x_0}\preceq_s e_x+\epsilon_ne_{x_1}$, because $R_{s-\epsilon_n}+\epsilon_ne_{x_1}=R_s+\epsilon_ne_{x_0}$. Let $K:=R_s^-$. Adding the fixed nonnegative map $K$ to both sides converts this signed comparison into the compound comparison $R_s^++\epsilon_ne_{x_0}\preceq e_x+K+\epsilon_ne_{x_1}$. Their bases have equal mass because $m(R_s^+)-m(K)=1=m(e_x)$. Stability with positive unit-mass spectators $e_{x_0},e_{x_1}$ yields $R_s^+\preceq e_x+K$, that is, $R_s\preceq_s e_x$.

Since $s$ is an upper bound, $s+\epsilon_n\notin L_x$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$. To derive the reverse signed comparison from CH, set $H_n:=R_{s+\epsilon_n}^-$. The translated maps $e_x+H_n$ and $R_{s+\epsilon_n}+H_n=R_{s+\epsilon_n}^+$ are nonnegative compounds. Since $R_{s+\epsilon_n}=R_{s+\epsilon_n}^+-H_n$ has total coefficient one, finite-sum linearity gives $m(R_{s+\epsilon_n}^+)-m(H_n)=1$; with $m(e_x)=1$, the translated compounds have equal mass $1+m(H_n)$. CH applies to this pair. If it gave $R_{s+\epsilon_n}^+\preceq e_x+H_n$, signed translation invariance in [F2] would imply $R_{s+\epsilon_n}\preceq_s e_x$, contrary to $s+\epsilon_n\notin L_x$. Therefore it gives $e_x+H_n\preceq R_{s+\epsilon_n}^+$, which by [F2] is $e_x\preceq_s R_{s+\epsilon_n}$. Add $\epsilon_ne_{x_0}$ to both signed maps and use $R_{s+\epsilon_n}+\epsilon_ne_{x_0}=R_s+\epsilon_ne_{x_1}$. Then add $K=R_s^-$ to both; the resulting equal-mass compound comparison is $e_x+K+\epsilon_ne_{x_0}\preceq R_s^++\epsilon_ne_{x_1}$. Stability with bases $e_x+K,R_s^+$ and positive unit-mass spectators $e_{x_0},e_{x_1}$ gives $e_x+K\preceq R_s^+$, or $e_x\preceq_sR_s$. Together with step 3.1 this proves $R_s\sim_s e_x$ and the claimed attainment.

Assume [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]] on compounds over a nonempty state set $X$, a strict reference pair $x_0\preceq x_1$ with not $x_1\preceq x_0$, and the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$. For $x\in X$ define

$$L_x:=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R:R_\lambda\preceq_s e_x\}.$$

Then $L_x$ is nonempty, bounded above, and downward closed. Its supremum $S(x):=\sup L_x$ is a real number and satisfies $R_{S(x)}\sim_s e_x$. Stability is used to prove attainment; no continuity of states or order is assumed.

A natural number is a von Neumann natural ([[def-natural-numbers]]), that is a
set, and $n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\} = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$
([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). Taking $X = n$ therefore gives

$$F^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to F \,\},$$

whose elements are written $x = (x_0, x_1, \dots, x_{n-1})$ with $x_i := x(i)$ for
$i < n$. **The coordinates are indexed from $0$**, because $0 \in n$ whenever
$n \ne 0$ and $n \notin n$ always. The operations read

$$(x + y)_i = x_i + y_i, \qquad (\lambda x)_i = \lambda x_i \qquad (i < n),$$

and the zero of $F^{n}$ is the tuple all of whose coordinates are $0_F$.

2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b, c \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ and $b > 0$ then $ab > 0$.
2. If $a > 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab < 0$.
3. If $a < 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab > 0$.
4. If $c > 0$ then $a < b \iff ac < bc$.
5. If $c < 0$ then $a < b \iff bc < ac$ (multiplication by a negative reverses order).

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.
For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \neq 0$, there exists $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n = \sigma(m)$. Equivalently, every natural number is either $0$ or a successor.

derivations.claim: If $b$ solves the system and $\lambda_j\ge0$ with $\sum_j\lambda_jc_j=0$, multiply row $j$ by $\lambda_j$ and add the finitely many inequalities. By [F3] each row inequality is preserved under its nonnegative multiplier. By the coordinatewise definitions in the Statement and finite-sum distributivity with Fubini from [F2], $\sum_{j<m}\lambda_j(c_j\cdot b)=(\sum_{j<m}\lambda_jc_j)\cdot b=0$. Hence $0\ge\sum_{j<m}\lambda_jh_j$. This proves necessity.

For sufficiency, prove by induction on $n$ the alternative: if the finite system has no solution, there is a nonnegative combination of its rows whose coefficient vector is zero and whose right side is positive. If $n=0$, every row has zero left side; infeasibility means some $h_j>0$, and that single row is the certificate. If $m=0$, the system is feasible, so this case cannot occur under the induction claim's antecedent.

Let $n>0$ and assume the alternative for $n'$ variables, where $n=\sigma(n')=n'\cup\{n'\}$ by [F5] and [[def-natural-numbers]]. For $c\in\mathbb R^n$ define $a\in\mathbb R^{n'}$ by $a(k):=c(k)$ for $k<n'$, and put $\alpha:=c(n')\in\mathbb R$; this separates its first $n'$ coordinates and its last coordinate. Conversely, each $u\in\mathbb R^{n'}$ and $t\in\mathbb R$ determine the unique $b\in\mathbb R^n$ with $b(k)=u(k)$ for $k<n'$ and $b(n')=t$. For every row $c_j$, define $a_j(k):=c_j(k)$ for $k<n'$ and $\alpha_j:=c_j(n')$. Partition the row indices into $P=\{j:\alpha_j>0\}$, $N=\{j:\alpha_j<0\}$, and $Z=\{j:\alpha_j=0\}$. Retain each row $(a_j,h_j)$ for $j\in Z$. For every $p\in P$ and $q\in N$, add the reduced row $((-\alpha_q)a_p+\alpha_p a_q,\;(-\alpha_q)h_p+\alpha_p h_q)$. Every multiplier used is positive, so these row combinations preserve the inequality directions by [F3].

The reduced system in $u\in\mathbb R^{n'}$ is feasible exactly when the original is, using the coordinate reconstruction in step 1.3. Indeed, a solution $(u,t)$ implies every retained inequality; adding row $p$ multiplied by $-\alpha_q>0$ to row $q$ multiplied by $\alpha_p>0$ cancels $t$ and gives each pair row. Conversely, if $u$ satisfies the reduced system, rows in $P$ impose finitely many lower bounds $t\ge L_p:=(h_p-a_p\cdot u)/\alpha_p$, and rows in $N$ impose finitely many upper bounds $t\le U_q:=(h_q-a_q\cdot u)/\alpha_q$. Each pair row is exactly $L_p\le U_q$. To justify the finite extrema, enumerate any nonempty finite list $\ell_0,\ldots,\ell_{k-1}$ of lower bounds and define $M_1=\ell_0$; for $1\le j<k$, recursively set $M_{j+1}=M_j$ if $M_j\ge\ell_j$, and $M_{j+1}=\ell_j$ otherwise. Totality of the real order makes $M_{j+1}$ the larger of $M_j$ and $\ell_j$; induction [F4] shows that $M_k$ is a member of the list and dominates every entry. Thus a finite nonempty list has a maximum. For an upper-bound list $v_0,\ldots,v_{\ell-1}$, define $m_1=v_0$ and, for $1\le j<\ell$, set $m_{j+1}=m_j$ if $m_j\le v_j$, and $m_{j+1}=v_j$ otherwise. The same totality and induction argument shows $m_\ell$ is a member no greater than any entry, so every finite nonempty list has a minimum. If both $P,N$ are nonempty, these extrema and all pair inequalities give $\max_{p\in P}L_p\le\min_{q\in N}U_q$, so choose $t=\max_{p\in P}L_p$. If only lower bounds occur choose their finite maximum; if only upper bounds occur choose their finite minimum; if neither occurs choose $t=0$. Thus the original system has a solution.

If the original system is infeasible, step 2.1 makes the reduced system infeasible. By induction there are nonnegative multipliers on reduced rows with zero combined first $n'$ coordinates and positive combined right side. Lift each retained zero-row multiplier to its original row; lift each pair-row multiplier $\mu_{pq}$ to coefficients $-\alpha_q\mu_{pq}$ on row $p$ and $\alpha_p\mu_{pq}$ on row $q$. All lifted coefficients are nonnegative by [F3]. Every pair lift has last coordinate $(-\alpha_q)\alpha_p+\alpha_p\alpha_q=0$; the total first coordinates vanish by the reduced certificate, and its right side remains positive. This is the required certificate for the original system and completes the induction.

If the stated multiplier condition holds, the certificate from step 3.1 cannot exist, because it would have zero combined left coefficient and positive combined right side. Therefore the system is feasible. Together with step 1.1 this proves both directions, including the empty-variable base case in step 1.2, the zero/positive/negative sign partition and bound reconstruction in steps 1.3–2.1, and the lifted certificate in step 3.1.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb N$ be finite, let $c_j\in\mathbb R^n$ and $h_j\in\mathbb R$ for $0\le j<m$, where $\mathbb R^n$ is the function space on $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ with coordinatewise operations as in [[def-function-space]]. For $c,b\in\mathbb R^n$, define the dot product by $c\cdot b:=\sum_{k<n}c(k)b(k)$. A finite vector sum is coordinatewise: $(\sum_{j<m}\lambda_jc_j)(k):=\sum_{j<m}\lambda_jc_j(k)$ for each $k<n$. All sums use [[def-finite-sum]].

The finite system

$$c_j\cdot b\ge h_j\qquad(0\le j<m)$$

has a solution $b\in\mathbb R^n$ if and only if every $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$ with $\lambda_j\ge0$ and $\sum_{j<m}\lambda_jc_j=0$ satisfies $\sum_{j<m}\lambda_jh_j\le0$. Dot products and sums are finite. This includes empty rows, empty variables, and an empty inequality family.

By [F2], choose a natural number $m$ and a bijection $\phi:m	o A$; when $A=\varnothing$, take $m=0$ and the empty bijection. Reindex the data as $c_j:=
u_{\phi(j)}$ and $h_j:=-d_{\phi(j)}$ for $j<m$. The row system $c_j\cdot b\ge h_j$ is exactly the required offset system. By [F1], it is feasible exactly when every nonnegative multiplier family $\mu\in\mathbb R^m$ with $\sum_{j<m}\mu_jc_j=0$ has $\sum_{j<m}\mu_jh_j\le0$. The bijection transports such a family to $\lambda_a:=\mu_{\phi^{-1}(a)}$ on $A$, preserving nonnegativity and both finite sums by [F2]. Hence this condition is precisely $\sum_{a\in A}\lambda_a
u_a=0\Rightarrow\sum_{a\in A}\lambda_ad_a\ge0$. For $A=\varnothing$, $b=0$ is feasible and the multiplier condition is vacuous. If $r=0$ and $A$ is nonempty, every $
u_a=0$; testing the coordinate multiplier for each channel makes the criterion equivalent to $d_a\ge0$ for every $a$, and then the unique empty vector $b$ satisfies all rows.

For any channel with actual change $\Delta\sigma_a\ge d_a$, add $b\cdot
u_a$ to both sides of that bound and use the solved row inequality $b\cdot
u_a\ge-d_a$. Then $\Delta\sigma_a+b\cdot
u_a\ge d_a+b\cdot
u_a\ge0$. This is a sufficient monotonicity conclusion for the stated channels.

citations.quote: The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

So $(W,+,0_V)$ is an abelian group, which is axiom (V1), and $W$ is a vector
space over $F$ **whose zero vector and whose additive inverses are those of
$V$**. In the language of [[def-subgroup]], the three displayed conditions
(S1) $0_V \in W$, (S2) closure under addition and (S3) closure under additive
inverses all hold, so $W$ is a subgroup of the abelian group $(V,+,0_V)$
([[def-group]]); that reading, and its converse, are recorded as
[[lem-linear-subspace-is-a-subgroup]] and are cited from there rather than
re-argued below.

Let $X$ be a real vector space ([[def-vector-space]]). A function
$p:X \to \mathbb{R}$ is a **sublinear functional** if

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a real vector space, let
$M \subseteq X$ be a linear subspace, let
$p:X \to \mathbb{R}$ be sublinear, and let $f:M \to \mathbb{R}$ be linear with
$f(m) \le p(m)$ for every $m \in M$. Then there exists a linear functional
$F:X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $F|_M=f$ and $F(x) \le p(x)$ for every $x \in X$.

- $u \in F$ is an **upper bound** of $S$ if $s \le u$ for all $s \in S$; $S$ is
  **bounded above** if it has an upper bound.
- $u \in F$ is a **least upper bound** (or **supremum**, $\sup S$) of $S$ if $u$
  is an upper bound of $S$ and $u \le u'$ for every upper bound $u'$ of $S$.

**Assume the Axiom of Choice**, through
[[thm-every-independent-set-extends-to-a-basis]]. Then every vector space $V$
over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) has a basis ([[def-linear-basis]]).

**Assume the Axiom of Choice** ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), which is what
[[thm-zorn]] is proved from. Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$
([[def-vector-space]]) and let $L \subseteq S \subseteq V$ with $L$ linearly
independent ([[def-linear-independence]]) and $\operatorname{span}(S) = V$
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]). Then there is a basis $B$ of $V$
([[def-linear-basis]]) with

- **The empty list is independent.** For $n = 0$ the only list of scalars is the
  empty one, and the condition "$\lambda_i = 0_F$ for every $i < 0$" holds
  vacuously.
- **$\varnothing \subseteq V$ is independent.** The only function $v : n \to
  \varnothing$ is the empty one, with $n = 0$, and it is independent by the
  previous point.
- **$\{0_V\}$ is dependent.** The list $v : 1 \to \{0_V\}$ with $v_0 = 0_V$ is
  injective, and taking $\lambda_0 = 1_F$ gives
  $\sum_{i<1}\lambda_i v_i = 0_V + 1_F 0_V = 0_V$ by the recursion of
  [[def-monoid-finite-product]] and $\lambda 0_V = 0_V$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), while $1_F \ne 0_F$ in a field
  ([[def-field]]). So $\{0_V\}$, and hence every subset of $V$ containing $0_V$,
  is linearly dependent.

- **(B1)** $B$ is linearly independent ([[def-linear-independence]]), and
- **(B2)** $B$ spans $V$, that is $\operatorname{span}(B) = V$
  ([[def-linear-combination-and-span]], which is where the words *spans* and
  *spanning set* are fixed; they are not redefined here).

The class of $c\in F$ is $[c]$. The defining relations are $[e_{\Gamma\times\Gamma'}]=[e_\Gamma]+[e_{\Gamma'}]$ and $[e_{t\Gamma}]=t[e_\Gamma]$. The set existence, subspace properties, quotient operations and vector-space laws are proved in [[lem-tdmath-type-offset-vector-space-well-defined]]. These are formal algebraic type labels; no actual catalyst-chain cost or physical existence claim is built into $V_{\mathcal G}$.

For the construction in [[def-tdmath-type-offset-vector-space]], $F$ and $N$ are sets, $F$ is a real vector space, $N$ is a linear subspace of $F$, and $F/N$ has representative-independent vector operations making it a real vector space. Its displayed product and positive-scaling relations hold in the quotient.

Fix two objects $-\infty$ and $+\infty$, distinct from one another and neither of
them a real number ([[def-real-numbers]]), and set

$$\overline{\mathbb{R}} := \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty, +\infty\}.$$

This is a **new object**, introduced here explicitly with its own order and its
own partial arithmetic. It is not an enlargement of the field $\mathbb{R}$, and
no operation of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) is redefined by
anything below.

**The order.** For $a, b \in \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ declare

$$a \le b \quad :\Longleftrightarrow \quad a = -\infty \ \text{ or } \ b = +\infty \ \text{ or } \ \big(a, b \in \mathbb{R} \text{ and } a \le b \text{ in } \mathbb{R}\big),$$

with $\mathbb{R}$ ordered as in [[def-real-order]], and write $a < b$ for
"$a \le b$ and $a \ne b$" as usual ([[def-partial-order]]).

**$(\overline{\mathbb{R}}, \le)$ is a totally ordered set, and the inclusion of
$\mathbb{R}$ preserves and reflects the order.** All four checks are immediate
from the displayed clauses.

- *Reflexive.* For $a = \pm\infty$ one of the first two clauses applies; for
  $a \in \mathbb{R}$ the third does, since $a \le a$ in $\mathbb{R}$.
- *Antisymmetric.* Suppose $a \le b$ and $b \le a$. If $a = -\infty$ then
  $b \le a$ forces $b = -\infty$, since the clause $a = +\infty$ fails and $b, a$
  are not both real. Symmetrically $b = -\infty$ forces $a = -\infty$, and
  $a = +\infty$ or $b = +\infty$ forces the other to be $+\infty$. In the one
  remaining situation $a$ and $b$ are both real and antisymmetry is that of
  $\mathbb{R}$.
- *Transitive.* Let $a \le b \le c$. If $a = -\infty$ or $c = +\infty$ the
  conclusion is one of the first two clauses. Otherwise $a \ne -\infty$ forces,
  in $a \le b$, either $b = +\infty$ or $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$; and $c \ne +\infty$
  forces, in $b \le c$, either $b = -\infty$ or $b, c \in \mathbb{R}$. The value
  $b = +\infty$ is incompatible with the second alternative pair, so $b$ is real,
  hence so are $a$ and $c$, and transitivity is that of $\mathbb{R}$.
- *Total.* If $a = -\infty$ or $b = +\infty$ then $a \le b$; if $b = -\infty$ or
  $a = +\infty$ then $b \le a$; otherwise both are real and the order of
  $\mathbb{R}$ is total.
- *Preserved and reflected.* For $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ the first two clauses fail,
  so $a \le b$ in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ says exactly $a \le b$ in $\mathbb{R}$.

In particular $-\infty$ is the least and $+\infty$ the greatest element of
$\overline{\mathbb{R}}$, and $-\infty < x < +\infty$ for every $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

**Reflection.** Extend negation by

$$-(+\infty) := -\infty, \qquad -(-\infty) := +\infty,$$

keeping the field negative on $\mathbb{R}$. The resulting map
$\nu : \overline{\mathbb{R}} \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$, $\nu(a) = -a$, satisfies
$\nu(\nu(a)) = a$ and

$$a \le b \iff -b \le -a \qquad (a, b \in \overline{\mathbb{R}}).$$

For $a$ and $b$ real this is the elementwise order reversal in $\mathbb{R}$:
translation invariance ([[lem-of-add-order]]) applied with the constant $-a-b$
turns $a < b$ into $-b < -a$ and, applied with the constant $a+b$, turns it back,
while $a = b$ holds exactly when $-a = -b$. In every other case both sides are
decided by the first two clauses of the order: $a = -\infty$ makes both sides
true, as does $b = +\infty$, and if $a \ne -\infty$, $b \ne +\infty$ and $a, b$
are not both real then one of $a = +\infty$, $b = -\infty$ holds and both sides
are false.

**Partial addition.** For $a, b \in \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ the sum $a + b$ is
defined by

- $a + b$ = the field sum, when $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$;
- $a + b := +\infty$ when $a = +\infty$ and $b \ne -\infty$, or $b = +\infty$ and $a \ne -\infty$;
- $a + b := -\infty$ when $a = -\infty$ and $b \ne +\infty$, or $b = -\infty$ and $a \ne +\infty$;

and **the two sums $(+\infty) + (-\infty)$ and $(-\infty) + (+\infty)$ are left
undefined**. Addition is commutative where defined, and

$$-(a + b) = (-a) + (-b),$$

each side being defined exactly when the other is: the excluded pairs
$\{+\infty, -\infty\}$ are exchanged by $\nu$, and the three clauses above are
exchanged accordingly.

**Partial multiplication.** For $a, b \in \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ the product $ab$
is defined by

- $ab$ = the field product, when $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$;
- $ab := +\infty$ when one of $a, b$ is $\pm\infty$, the other is $\ne 0$, and both are $> 0$ or both are $< 0$;
- $ab := -\infty$ when one of $a, b$ is $\pm\infty$, the other is $\ne 0$, and one is $> 0$ and the other $< 0$;

and **every product with one factor $0$ and the other $\pm\infty$ is left
undefined**. The comparisons $> 0$ and $< 0$ here are taken in the order above,
under which $+\infty > 0 > -\infty$.

**Nothing else is defined.** There is no subtraction, no division, no
exponentiation and no absolute value on $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ in this library;
where such an expression is wanted it is written out in the two defined
operations, and where a case falls in the undefined list the statement carries an
explicit hypothesis saying so.

Let $V$ be a vector space over $F$. A **linear functional** on $V$ is a linear map $f:V\to F$, where $F$ is regarded as a vector space over itself. The **algebraic dual space** of $V$ is

$$V^*:=\mathcal L(V,F),$$

with pointwise addition and scalar multiplication. This is the full algebraic dual: no topology, norm, or continuity condition is imposed.

Let $\varphi(z, \bar p)$ be a formula of the language of set theory
([[def-language-of-set-theory]]) in which the variable $y$ does not occur free.
The **Separation instance** for $\varphi$ is the sentence

$$\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,\bigl(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p))\bigr).$$

The **Axiom Schema of Separation** is the collection of all these sentences, one
for each such $\varphi$. In words: for any parameters $\bar p$ and any set $x$,
there is a set $y$ whose elements are exactly the elements $z$ of $x$ for which
$\varphi(z,\bar p)$ holds.

It is a schema and not a single axiom because $\varphi$ ranges over the formulas
of the language, of which there are infinitely many, and the language provides no
way to quantify over them.

derivations.claim: By [F10], $W$ is a set. It contains $0$ because $p(0)=0$. If $x,y\in W$, subadditivity gives $p(x+y)\le p(x)+p(y)<+\infty$, so $x+y\in W$ by the extended-real conventions in [F8]. For $t>0$, homogeneity gives $p(tx)=tp(x)<+\infty$. If $t<0$, put $s:=-t>0$; no-sinks gives $-x\in W$, and positive homogeneity applied to $s(-x)=tx$ puts $tx$ in $W$. Also $0x=0\in W$. Thus $W$ is a linear subspace. The restriction $p|_W$ is finite-valued, positively homogeneous and subadditive, so it is a real-valued sublinear functional.

Let $M=\{0\}\subseteq W$ and let $f_0(0)=0$. This is linear and satisfies $f_0(0)=0=p(0)$. The real ordered field is complete by [F4], as used in the one-step interval argument of the published theorem. Apply [F3] to $p|_W$ and $f_0$; it gives a linear $\ell:W\to\mathbb R$ with $\ell(x)\le p(x)$ for every $x\in W$. Applying this at $-x\in W$ yields $-\ell(x)=\ell(-x)\le p(-x)$, so $-p(-x)\le\ell(x)\le p(x)$ on $W$.

By [F5], choose a basis $B_W$ of $W$ and extend its independent set to a basis $B_V$ of $V$. Assign value $\ell(b)$ to $b\in B_W$ and $0$ to $b\in B_V\setminus B_W$. For any $v\in V$, [F6] gives a finite basis expression; define $L(v)$ as the same finite linear combination of assigned real values. If two expressions represented $v$, subtracting and collecting equal basis vectors would give a finite zero combination; independence in [F6] forces every collected coefficient to be zero. Thus $L(v)$ is well-defined. Concatenating finite expressions proves additivity and scalar homogeneity, so $L$ is linear in the sense of [F9]; the basis expression of any $w\in W$ uses only $B_W$, so $L|_W=\ell$.

For $x\in W$, step 3.1 and step 2.1 give $-p(-x)\le L(x)\le p(x)$. If $x\notin W$, then $p(x)=+\infty$ by the definition of $W$; no-sinks implies $p(-x)=+\infty$ as well, so by [F8] the extended bounds reduce to $-\infty\le L(x)\le+\infty$. This proves the global sandwich.

In the type-offset application, linearity of $L$ in the sense of [F9] and the quotient relations in [F7] give $B(\Gamma\times\Gamma')=B(\Gamma)+B(\Gamma')$ and $B(t\Gamma)=tB(\Gamma)$. Apply the sandwich to $e_\Gamma-e_{\Gamma'}$ and its negative, using the assumed values of $p$, to obtain the two displayed bounds for $B(\Gamma)-B(\Gamma')$. For an admitted transition, its real baseline change is at least $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$, so that cost value must be finite. The corrected change equals $[\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)-\sigma_\Gamma(x)] + B(\Gamma')-B(\Gamma)=[\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)-\sigma_\Gamma(x)]-L(e_\Gamma-e_{\Gamma'})$. The assumed lower bound on the baseline change and the upper sandwich bound $L(e_\Gamma-e_{\Gamma'})\le F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$ make this at least $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')-F(\Gamma,\Gamma')=0$. This proves only the stated conditional monotonicity.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $V$ be a real vector space and $p:V\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ satisfy $p(0)=0$, $p(tx)=tp(x)$ for every $t>0$, and $p(x+y)\le p(x)+p(y)$ in extended-real arithmetic. Assume **no sinks**: $p(x)<+\infty$ if and only if $p(-x)<+\infty$. Put $W:=\{x\in V:p(x)<+\infty\}$. Then $W$ is a linear subspace and there exists a real-linear $L:V\to\mathbb R$ such that

$$-p(-x)\le L(x)\le p(x)\qquad(x\in V),$$

with $-\infty\le r\le+\infty$ interpreted in the usual extended order. The result is valid in arbitrary dimension and allows $p=+\infty$ outside $W$.

For the conditional offset application, let $V=V_{\mathcal G}$ from [[def-tdmath-type-offset-vector-space]], let $F:\mathcal G\times\mathcal G\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ satisfy $p([e_\Gamma]-[e_{\Gamma'}])=F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$, and define $B(\Gamma):=L([e_\Gamma])$. Then $B(\Gamma\times\Gamma')=B(\Gamma)+B(\Gamma')$, $B(t\Gamma)=tB(\Gamma)$ for $t>0$, and

$$-F(\Gamma',\Gamma)\le B(\Gamma)-B(\Gamma')\le F(\Gamma,\Gamma').$$

For each $\Gamma\in\mathcal G$, let $X_\Gamma$ be a state set and $\sigma_\Gamma:X_\Gamma\to\mathbb R$ a baseline state function. If every admitted transition $(\Gamma,x)\to(\Gamma',y)$, with $x\in X_\Gamma$ and $y\in X_{\Gamma'}$, satisfies $\sigma_{\Gamma'}(y)-\sigma_\Gamma(x)\ge F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$, then $\sigma_\Gamma(x)+B(\Gamma)$ is nondecreasing across those transitions. The existence or properties of such a cost $p$, including no-sinks, are hypotheses and are not proved by this theorem.

boundaries.evidence: 4.1 treats x outside W, where both bounds are infinite.
4.1 and 5.1 preserve extended-real endpoints and require finite cost on admitted transitions.
3.1 explicitly uses AC for bases and basis extension.
Statement no-sinks is an assumed finiteness biconditional, not a theorem about an arbitrary cost. Step 1.1 uses forward finiteness to put the negated vector in W.
