citations.quote:
**(a) Adopted readings and framework data.** Adopt the state and composition
postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]] (P1), the observable
and probability postulate
[[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]] (P2), the
autonomous-dynamics postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-autonomous-dynamics]]
(P4) and the preparation and apparatus postulate
[[post-nrqm-framework-preparation-and-apparatus]] (P7), together with the
Boltzmann-constant and temperature conventions of
[[def-nrqm-many-body-framework-entropy-and-free-energy]]. Declare one of the
following model readings of the same **adopted Gibbs assignment**:

(i) a fixed-$N$ model of
[[def-nrqm-many-body-framework-declared-fixed-n-model]], on its sector space,
with Gibbs generator $G:=H_N^\sigma$; or

(ii) a separately declared number-variable mode model, such as a one-mode
bosonic Fock space, a fermionic occupation space, or a declared countable
independent-mode space, with its declared assigned observables and energy
operator $H$. The model declares a self-adjoint Gibbs generator $G$ on that
space: either $G=H$, or a separately supplied self-adjoint realization of the
effective generator $G=H-\mu\mathcal N$, where $\mathcal N$ is the declared
particle-number operator and $\mu\in\mathbb R$ is an assigned chemical
potential in joules. The subtraction is an operator with its supplied domain,
not an assertion that a formal unbounded difference is self-adjoint.

In either reading assume $G$ is bounded below and give its spectral PVM
$E_G$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]],
[[def-projection-valued-measure]]). Let $T>0$ be an assigned temperature in
kelvin and let $\beta:=1/(k_BT)$ in $\mathrm J^{-1}$ with the assigned
Boltzmann constant $k_B$. The Gibbs assignment to either model, and the
chemical-potential identification in (ii), are additional physical
preparation assumptions made here; they are not derived from P1-P4 or from
the fixed-$N$ construction. In (ii) no restriction on the assigned real
$\mu$ is imposed beyond the declared generator and trace existence
conditions; the mode-specific convergence conditions are proved separately.
For reading (ii), $G$ specifies the Gibbs weights. If the assigned autonomous
dynamics is generated by $H$, stationarity of the Gibbs density requires its
separate dynamical or commutation hypotheses; this assignment does not
identify $H-\mu\mathcal N$ with the physical evolution generator.
The physical Helmholtz free-energy vocabulary of the entropy definition
continues to apply only to its stated nonzero finite-sector class and is not
extended to every effective generator by this postulate.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), the choice hypotheses of
the spectral calculus.

**(b) Existence hypothesis and the Gibbs preparation.** The model assumes
that the **partition trace is strictly positive and finite**:
$$0<Z:=\operatorname{Tr}e^{-\beta G}<\infty,$$
where $\operatorname{Tr}B:=\sum_{f\in\mathcal B}\langle Bf,f\rangle$ for a
bounded positive $B$ and an orthonormal basis $\mathcal B$, with value allowed
to be $+\infty$. Such a basis exists under the declared AC by the maximal
orthonormal-family argument using [[thm-zorn]] and the zero-complement
criterion of [[thm-parseval-equivalences-for-a-complete-orthonormal-family]].
This trace is basis independent: for $C:=B^{1/2}$ of
[[thm-positive-square-root]], the defining sum is
$\sum_{f\in\mathcal B}\|Cf\|^2$, whose invariance is
[[thm-hilbert-schmidt-norm-is-basis-independent]]. When the sum is finite,
$C$ is Hilbert-Schmidt ([[def-hilbert-schmidt-operator]]), so $B=C^2$ is
trace class by [[thm-trace-class-iff-product-of-two-hilbert-schmidt-operators]],
and its ordinary trace is this same diagonal sum by
[[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]. Apply this to the bounded positive operator $e^{-\beta G}$, since the
declared Gibbs generator $G$ is bounded below. The model
adopts as the **canonical** or **Gibbs preparation** of the declared model
at temperature $T$ the density operator
$$\rho_\beta:=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta G}.$$
If the sector is zero-dimensional, its partition trace is $Z=0$, no
trace-one density exists, and no canonical density or equilibrium free
energy is assigned. On a nonzero finite-dimensional model space, $Z$ is a
positive finite sum $\sum_je^{-\beta E_j}$ over the eigenvalues of $G$; no energy
sign restriction is needed. There $\rho_\beta$ is the canonical operator of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-finite-gibbs-free-energy-minimum]], and the
strict positivity and finiteness hypothesis is automatic. In reading (i),
$Z=Z_N$ and this is precisely the finite-sector Gibbs assignment.

Outside the finite-dimensional class the existence hypothesis is a genuine
restriction. For a declared non-interacting fixed-$N$ model with a supplied
countably infinite orthonormal eigenmode basis and real mode energies
$\varepsilon_j$ bounded below, the complete construction and trace criterion
of [[lem-nrqm-many-body-fixed-n-countable-mode-partition-criterion]] give
$Z_N=h_N(q)$ for bosonic statistics or $Z_N=e_N(q)$ for fermionic statistics,
where $q_j=e^{-\beta\varepsilon_j}$ and $h_N,e_N$ are the corresponding
nonnegative occupation-series sums. For every fixed $N\ge1$, either trace is
finite exactly when $\sum_jq_j<\infty$. This is a trace on the fixed-$N$
sector and permits negative mode energies.

For the separately declared full bosonic Fock models of reading (ii),
the single-mode calculation of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-single-mode-thermal-trace]] and the product
criterion of [[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-countable-mode-product-criterion]]
provide the separate mathematical full-Fock traces, with their original
positive mode-energy hypotheses: they sum over every particle number,
including the vacuum, giving $(1-e^{-\beta\varepsilon})^{-1}$ for one mode
and $\prod_j(1-e^{-\beta\varepsilon_j})^{-1}$ for countably many modes.
Their physical Gibbs reading is the additional assignment of (a)(ii), not a
consequence of a mathematical trace formula. Those full-Fock traces are not
substituted for the fixed-$N$ partition trace of reading (i).

**(c) The equilibrium assumption and thermal means.** The model **assumes**
that, for a declared sample of the species at the assigned temperature $T$
and in the absence of further preparation information, the preparation
description of the sample is $\rho_\beta$ in the sense of P1. For an assigned
sharp observable $(A,u_A)$ with spectral PVM $E_A$, define its outcome law
$\mu_{\rho_\beta}^A(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\beta E_A(B))$ as in
[[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] clause (b).
If and only if the absolute first moment is finite,
$$\int_{\mathbb R}|a|\,d\mu_{\rho_\beta}^A(a)<\infty,$$
the model defines the **thermal mean** at temperature $T$ by
$$\langle A\rangle_\beta:=\int_{\mathbb R}a\,d\mu_{\rho_\beta}^A(a),$$
read in the assigned unit $u_A$. For bounded $A$ this equals
$\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\beta A)=\operatorname{tr}(A\rho_\beta)$. For
unbounded $A$, if the mean exists and the literal product $A\rho_\beta$ is
defined on the whole Hilbert space and is trace class, the mean also equals
$\operatorname{tr}(A\rho_\beta)$ and
$\operatorname{tr}(\overline{\rho_\beta A})$; these conditional product
identities are proved by the density eigenexpansion in
[[lem-nrqm-many-body-spectral-mean-and-defined-trace-product]]. First-moment
existence alone imposes no such product or operator-square-domain condition.
When the absolute first moment is infinite the model asserts no finite
thermal mean. The identification of the parameter $T$ with the thermodynamic temperature of a
sample, and of $\beta$ with its inverse temperature, is part of this
assumption; the stated conservation and equilibrium properties of
$\rho_\beta$ under the flow of P4, and the extremal property of $\rho_\beta$
among preparations, are separate conditional results of this pair.

**(d) Motivation and status.** The assumption is motivated, but not
established, by the maximum-entropy reasoning of the cited sources: among
preparations with a prescribed mean energy, the Gibbs weights maximize the
entropy functional, and the finite-dimensional comparison theorem makes
$\rho_\beta$ the minimizer of the corresponding functional built from $G$.
Its physical Helmholtz free-energy reading applies in the stated finite
fixed-sector class; an effective-generator interpretation in a different
mode model is a separate declared reading. That reasoning is
an argument inside mathematical statistics and thermodynamics; it does not
derive the physical assumption that a sample is described by $\rho_\beta$.
The postulate is an **adopted** statistical-mechanical assumption of the
model, in the sense of the content model's distinction between adopted
assumptions and derived consequences.

**(e) Scope.** The postulate asserts nothing about how a sample reaches the
Gibbs preparation; in particular it asserts no thermalization, no equilibration
time, no ergodicity, no master-equation or Markov approximation, no
thermodynamic limit, no pressure, volume or phase-transition structure, and
no measured temperature or expectation. The requirement $0<Z<\infty$ is part
of the assumption; the model does not define a canonical preparation when
$Z=0$ or the partition trace diverges. Any comparison with a laboratory sample requires the
declared preparation, isolation, detection and sampling models of P7, and
agreement of a thermal prediction with data is evidence about the combined
model and apparatus assumptions, not a proof of the framework or of this
postulate.

Assume AC and Countable Choice and adopt the quantum Gibbs preparation of [[post-nrqm-many-body-canonical-equilibrium-ensemble]] at assigned temperature $T>0$ kelvins, with $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T)^{-1}$ in $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$. A finite independent mode list means an integer $m\ge1$ and, for each $r\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$, a declared type B or F and an excitation energy $\varepsilon_r>0$ joules. For type B take the one-mode Fock Hilbert space with complete number basis $(e_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_0}$ and self-adjoint occupation operator $N_re_n=ne_n$ on its exact diagonal domain as in [[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-single-mode-thermal-trace]]. For type F take $\mathcal H_r=\mathbb C^2$ with orthonormal basis $f_0,f_1$ and $N_rf_n=nf_n$. In either case put $H_r=\varepsilon_rN_r$, and write $u_{r,n}=e_n$ or $f_n$ according to the factor type. Define $\mathcal H^{(1)}=\mathcal H_1$ and recursively $\mathcal H^{(r+1)}=\mathcal H^{(r)}\widehat\otimes\mathcal H_{r+1}$ by the completed Hilbert tensor construction of [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]; let $\mathcal H=\mathcal H^{(m)}$. The canonical orthonormal product basis is $u_{\mathbf n}=\bigotimes_r u_{r,n_r}$, indexed by $\mathbf n=(n_1,\ldots,n_m)\in\mathcal C:=\prod_r\mathcal C_r$, where $\mathcal C_r=\mathbb N_0$ for type B and $\mathcal C_r=\{0,1\}$ for type F. If all factors are F then $\mathcal C$ is finite; otherwise it is countably infinite and is enumerated by increasing $\sum_r n_r$ and lexicographic order within each finite level, which is finite because every $n_r\le\sum_r n_r$. For each factor put $\hat\varepsilon_r=\varepsilon_r/(1\,\mathrm J)$. Define the numerical energy map $\hat E:\mathcal C\to\mathbb R$ by $\hat E(\mathbf n)=\sum_{r=1}^m\hat\varepsilon_rn_r$ and the physical energy $E(\mathbf n)=(1\,\mathrm J)\hat E(\mathbf n)$. Define the numerical self-adjoint diagonal operator $\hat H$ by $\hat Hu_{\mathbf n}=\hat E(\mathbf n)u_{\mathbf n}$ on the exact domain
$$D(\hat H)=\Bigl\{\psi\in\mathcal H:\sum_{\mathbf n\in\mathcal C}\hat E(\mathbf n)^2|\langle\psi,u_{\mathbf n}\rangle|^2<\infty\Bigr\};$$
when $\mathcal C$ is finite, $\hat H$ is a finite real diagonal endomorphism and is self-adjoint; when $\mathcal C$ is countably infinite, the diagonal-operator lemma [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] gives $\hat H$ self-adjoint for the displayed enumeration. The physical total energy operator is $H=(1\,\mathrm J)\hat H$, with $Hu_{\mathbf n}=E(\mathbf n)u_{\mathbf n}$ and $D(H)=D(\hat H)$; multiplication by a nonzero real scalar preserves self-adjointness.
This sum-energy Hamiltonian with no interaction term is the definition of independence for this quantum model.

For one bosonic mode with excitation energy $\varepsilon>0$ joules, let $q=e^{-\beta\varepsilon}$ and let $N$ be its dimensionless occupation number. Its partition trace and mean occupation are
$$Z_B=(1-q)^{-1},\qquad \langle N\rangle_B=\frac{q}{1-q}=\frac1{e^{\beta\varepsilon}-1}.$$
For a fermionic two-level occupation system with energies $0,\varepsilon$, the partition sum and excited-state occupation are
$$Z_F=1+q,\qquad \langle N\rangle_F=\frac{q}{1+q}=\frac1{e^{\beta\varepsilon}+1}.$$
For a finite independent collection as defined above, write $K_\beta=e^{-\beta H}$ and $Z=\operatorname{Tr}K_\beta$. Then $0<Z<\infty$ and the joint occupation-basis law is $P_\beta(\mathbf n):=e^{-\beta E(\mathbf n)}/Z$. For each factor $r$, define its marginal law by $P_{\beta,r}(k):=\sum_{\mathbf n\in\mathcal C:\,n_r=k}P_\beta(\mathbf n)$. The trace satisfies $Z=\prod_{r=1}^m Z_r$, the joint law factorizes as $P_\beta(\mathbf n)=\prod_{r=1}^m(q_r^{n_r}/Z_r)$, and each marginal mean is the corresponding one-mode mean displayed above. These are exact model identities under the adopted preparation.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statement of isolated autonomous dynamics. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), which are the choice hypotheses of the cited spectral and group suppliers.

**(i) Energy operator.** An **isolated autonomous system** of the sector has a declared **energy operator** $H_{\mathrm{op}}:D(H_{\mathrm{op}})\subset H\to H$ that is self-adjoint ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]) and a declared energy unit in which its spectral coordinate is read. The energy operator is part of the model specification of the system; for a massive particle it is fixed by the kinematics postulate P5, and singular or unbounded model Hamiltonians require their own self-adjointness statements.

**(ii) Evolution.** The time evolution of the model is the strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group
$$U(t):=\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{i}{\hbar}tH_{\mathrm{op}}\Bigr)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R),\qquad U(t+s)=U(t)U(s),\quad U(t)^{*}=U(t)^{-1},$$
defined by the spectral calculus of the self-adjoint generator ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]], [[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]], [[def-strongly-continuous-one-parameter-unitary-group]]). The energy unit enters the argument of the exponential so that $H_{\mathrm{op}}t/\hbar$ acts in the dimensionless spectral variable.

**(iii) State evolution.** A vector state evolves continuously, $\psi(t):=U(t)\psi(0)$ for every $\psi(0)\in H$, and the Schroedinger equation
$$i\hbar\,\frac{d}{dt}\psi(t)=H_{\mathrm{op}}\psi(t)$$
holds in the norm-differentiable sense exactly for initial vectors $\psi(0)\in D(H_{\mathrm{op}})$, where the derivative is the norm limit of the difference quotients; for other vectors the equation is not asserted, although the evolution remains continuous. A density-operator preparation evolves as $\rho(t)=U(t)\rho(0)U(t)^{*}$, which is a density operator for every $t$ and satisfies $\operatorname{tr}\rho(t)=1$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]).

**(iv) Time-dependent families.** A prescribed time-dependent family $t\mapsto H(t)$ of self-adjoint operators is a different model assumption: a norm-continuous finite-dimensional Hermitian family is used only through the unitary two-time propagator that its family defines, and the exponential of the integral of $H(t)$ is not identified with that propagator unless the family commutes with itself at different times. The general unbounded time-dependent case requires a separate existence and domain theorem of its own and is not adopted by this postulate; the driven-dynamics page states its own assumptions for the models it treats.

**(v) Open systems.** A non-unitary evolution of the reduced description of a system coupled to an environment is an extension obtained from an explicitly chosen environment model and a declared reduction, not a replacement for clause (ii); no environment model is adopted by this postulate.

**(vi) Status.** Clauses (i)-(v) are adopted assumptions of the isolated-system idealization. They assert nothing about the origin of the energy operator of a concrete system, about the accuracy of the idealization for a laboratory preparation, or about which laboratory interactions realize an isolated evolution; those are tested identifications in the sense of P7.

**(a) Assigned energy observable.** Adopt the autonomous-dynamics postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-autonomous-dynamics]] (P4) for a declared isolated system whose state space is the model's [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]]. An **assigned energy observable** of the system is an assigned sharp observable $(H_{\mathrm{op}},u_H)$ in the sense of [[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] clause (a), whose declared unit $u_H$ is an energy unit in the sense of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]] (joules in the SI conventions fixed there). Thus $H_{\mathrm{op}}:D(H_{\mathrm{op}})\subset H\to H$ is densely defined and self-adjoint ([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]], [[def-hilbert-space]]), with spectral projection-valued measure $E_H$ on the Borel sets of $\mathbb R$ under the choice hypotheses of [[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]] ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and its outcome law in a preparation is the law of [[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] clause (b). The assignment of $H_{\mathrm{op}}$ is part of the model specification, as in clause (i) of P4; this definition asserts nothing about which laboratory quantity of a concrete system realizes it.

**(b) The unitary flow.** The **time evolution** or **flow** of the isolated system is the family
$$U(t):=\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{i}{\hbar}tH_{\mathrm{op}}\Bigr):=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-it\lambda/\hbar}\,dE_H(\lambda)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R),$$
the reading of clause (ii) of P4 in the spectral calculus of $H_{\mathrm{op}}$ ([[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]]); here $\hbar>0$ is the reduced Planck constant with its value and unit fixed by [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]], so that $tH_{\mathrm{op}}/\hbar$ is dimensionless. Equivalently, $U(t)=e^{itT}$ for the self-adjoint generator $T:=-H_{\mathrm{op}}/\hbar$ with $D(T)=D(H_{\mathrm{op}})$; the two readings agree by the uniqueness of the generator in Stone's theorem, and by [[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]] ([[lem-nrqm-autonomous-dynamics-flow-calculus]] clause (a)) the family $U$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group: $U(0)=I$, $U(t+s)=U(t)U(s)$, $U(t)^{*}=U(t)^{-1}=U(-t)$ ([[def-strongly-continuous-one-parameter-unitary-group]]).

**(c) Schroedinger picture.** The **Schroedinger-picture evolution** of a preparation is fixed by clause (iii) of P4. A state vector evolves by $\psi(t):=U(t)\psi(0)$ for every $\psi(0)\in H$, and the **state at time $t$** of the pure preparation $[\psi(0)]$ is the pure preparation $[\psi(t)]$, which is well defined because $U(t)$ is injective; a general preparation $\rho$, that is an element of the state space $D(H)$ of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]], evolves by
$$\rho(t):=U(t)\rho(0)U(t)^{*},$$
the reading of clause (iii) of P4 in the density-operator vocabulary of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]] ([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]). In this picture the assigned observables are held fixed at their assigned values and the preparation moves.

**(d) Heisenberg picture.** For a **bounded** assigned sharp observable $(A,u_A)$ — that is, an assigned sharp observable with $A\in\mathcal B(H)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]), so that $A$ is self-adjoint and everywhere defined — the **Heisenberg representative** of $(A,u_A)$ at time $t$ is the pair $(A_H(t),u_A)$ with the same declared unit and
$$A_H(t):=U(t)^{*}AU(t)=U(-t)AU(t).$$
By [[lem-nrqm-autonomous-dynamics-heisenberg-flow]] clauses (a) and (d), $A_H(t)$ is again bounded and self-adjoint with spectral projection-valued measure $E_{A_H(t)}(B)=U(-t)E_A(B)U(t)$, so $(A_H(t),u_A)$ is again an assigned sharp observable of the framework; in this picture the preparation is held fixed at its value at time $0$ and the observables move. The two pictures are two bookkeeping devices for the same model; the statement that they assign the same outcome laws is proved in the Heisenberg-picture theorem of this page, not assumed here.

**(e) Stationary preparations.** A preparation $\rho\in D(H)$ is **stationary** for the assigned energy observable when $\rho(t)=\rho$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$. A pure preparation $[\psi]$ is stationary when $[\psi(t)]=[\psi(0)]$ for every $t$, that is, when the evolved vector remains in the ray of $\psi$; the characterization of this condition by the eigenrays of $H_{\mathrm{op}}$ is proved in the stationary-states theorem of this page, not assumed here. An **energy eigenstate** is a pure preparation of a unit eigenvector of $H_{\mathrm{op}}$, and a **stationary state** in the model is a stationary pure preparation; by that theorem the two notions coincide.

**(f) Energy-compatible observables.** An assigned sharp observable $(A,u_A)$ is **compatible with the energy**, or **energy-compatible**, when its spectral projection-valued measure and that of the energy commute strongly,
$$E_A(B)E_H(C)=E_H(C)E_A(B)\qquad\text{for all Borel }B,C\subseteq\mathbb R .$$
This is an equality of bounded operators on $H$, not a relation between formal commutators on a small domain; the phrase **conserved quantity** for an energy-compatible assigned observable is a claim about the time invariance of its outcome law and is established in the energy-conservation theorem of this page for bounded $A$.

**(g) Status.** Clauses (a)-(f) record the readings of P4 together with P1 and P2 in the vocabulary of this page and fix the terminology used by the later pages of the category. They adopt no physical assumption beyond P4, P1 and P2 and the choice hypotheses of the cited mathematics, assert no dynamics for a prescribed time-dependent family or for an open system (clauses (iv) and (v) of P4 are separate model assumptions treated on their own pages), assert no measurement model, no apparatus realization and no empirical result, and make no claim that any laboratory system is exactly isolated.

derivations.claim: The product trace in [F2] is $Z=(1+q)^2=9/4$. By the Gibbs assignment [F1] and the product-basis energies from the Statement, $P(n_1,n_2)=q^{n_1+n_2}/Z$; at $q=1/2$, the probabilities on $(00,01,10,11)$ are $(4/9,2/9,2/9,1/9)$. In particular, the Gibbs probability of $|11\rangle$ is $1/9>0$.

Since $H|00\rangle=0$, $U_t|00\rangle=|00\rangle$ for every $t$; thus $\rho(t)=|00\rangle\langle00|$. Its probability for the projector $|11\rangle\langle11|$ is zero at every time, unlike the Gibbs value $1/9$. The state therefore never reaches this Gibbs density under the declared unitary evolution.

Assume AC and Countable Choice for the canonical mode preparation. Let $\mathcal H_1=\mathcal H_2=\mathbb C^2$ with orthonormal basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$, and define the factor number maps by $N_r|0\rangle=0$, $N_r|1\rangle=|1\rangle$. The composite Hilbert space is the finite Hilbert tensor product $\mathcal H_1\widehat\otimes\mathcal H_2\cong\mathbb C^4$ from [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], with orthonormal product basis $|n_1n_2\rangle$, $n_r\in\{0,1\}$. On this basis define the site-number operators $\mathcal N_1|n_1n_2\rangle=n_1|n_1n_2\rangle$ and $\mathcal N_2|n_1n_2\rangle=n_2|n_1n_2\rangle$. For $T>0$ kelvins set $\varepsilon=k_{\mathrm B}T\log2$ joules and define the noninteracting total Hamiltonian
$$H=\varepsilon(\mathcal N_1+\mathcal N_2),\qquad H|n_1n_2\rangle=\varepsilon(n_1+n_2)|n_1n_2\rangle.$$
The quantum Gibbs preparation at $T$ is used for the thermal comparison, and the closed-system unitary evolution is generated by $H$ with $U_t=e^{-itH/\hbar}$, where $t$ is in seconds and $\hbar>0$ is in $\mathrm{J\,s}$. Start the dynamics in $\rho_0=|00\rangle\langle00|$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then:

1. If $(X,d_X)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]), the image
   $f[X] \subseteq Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$.
2. More generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$, then $f[K]$ is
   a compact subset of $Y$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ use the conventions of [[def-tdmath-extended-convex-function]]. Then $f$ is convex if and only if $\operatorname{epi}f$ is a convex subset of $\mathbb R^{d+1}$, and $f$ is lower semicontinuous if and only if $\operatorname{epi}f$ is closed.

A subset $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **convex** when, for all $x,y\in U$ and $t\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]), the point $(1-t)x+ty$ lies in $U$. Thus the full line segment from $x$ to $y$ remains in $U$.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be closed, proper, and convex in the sense of [[def-tdmath-extended-convex-function]]. With the Fenchel conjugate and biconjugate of [[def-tdmath-fenchel-transform-and-subgradient]], one has

$$f^{**}(x)=f(x)\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^d).$$

Let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be proper, let $x\in\operatorname{dom}f$, and let $p\in\mathbb R^d$. Then $f^*(p)\ge\langle p,x\rangle-f(x)$. Equality holds exactly when $p\in\partial f(x)$, equivalently when $x$ attains the supremum defining $f^*(p)$; in that case the supremum is finite.

For every linear $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ there is a unique matrix $A=(a_{ij})_{i<n,j<m}$ such that $(Lh)_i=\sum_{j<m}a_{ij}h_j$. Moreover there is $K\ge0$ with $\|Lh\|_2\le K\|h\|_2$ for every $h$.

derivations.claim: The set $\Delta_m$ contains each coordinate vector. The coordinate maps, the sum map $\theta\mapsto\sum_i\theta_i$, and $Q$ are continuous by [L1]. For any continuous map $T$ into a Euclidean space and any closed set $K$, the complement of $T^{-1}(K)$ is open: if $T(z)\notin K$, a ball about $T(z)$ misses $K$, and continuity gives a ball about $z$ mapped inside that ball. Thus $T^{-1}(K)$ is closed. Coordinate half-lines $[0,\infty)$ and singletons are closed, since a point outside either has a positive-distance ball missing it; a finite intersection of closed sets is closed because its complement is a finite union of open sets. These facts show that $\Delta_m$ is closed and that $\Theta_x=\Delta_m\cap Q^{-1}(\{x\})$ is closed. Since $0\le\theta_i\le1$ on $\Delta_m$, both sets are bounded and hence compact by [F1]. For $x\in P$, the definition of $P$ makes $\Theta_x$ nonempty. The linear objective is continuous by [L1] and attains its minimum on $\Theta_x$ by [F3].

Let $C=\{\sum_i\theta_i(q_i,a_i):\theta\in\Delta_m\}\subset\mathbb R^{d+1}$ and $V=\{(0,s):s\ge0\}$. The affine map defining $C$ is continuous by [L1], so $C$ is compact by [F2]. The set $C$ is convex because convex combinations of points in $\Delta_m$ remain in $\Delta_m$ (nonnegativity and the unit-sum equation are preserved) and the defining map is affine; $V$ is closed and convex. If $(x,r)\in\operatorname{epi}f_{\rm mix}$, a minimizing $\theta\in\Theta_x$ gives $(x,f_{\rm mix}(x))\in C$ and $r-f_{\rm mix}(x)\ge0$, so $(x,r)\in C+V$. Conversely if $(x,r)=\sum_i\theta_i(q_i,a_i)+(0,s)$ with $s\ge0$, then $f_{\rm mix}(x)\le\sum_i\theta_i a_i\le r$. Thus $\operatorname{epi}f_{\rm mix}=C+V$.

The coordinate vector with $\theta_i=1$ and all other weights zero shows $f_{\rm mix}(q_i)\le a_i$. Let $h:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be convex with $h(q_i)\le a_i$. For any weights $\theta\in\Delta_m$, prove $h(\sum_i\theta_iq_i)\le\sum_i\theta_i h(q_i)$ by induction on the number $N$ of positive weights: for $N=1$ it is equality; for $N>1$, choose an index $j$ with $0<\theta_j<1$, put $y=(1-\theta_j)^{-1}\sum_{i\ne j}\theta_iq_i$, and apply the induction hypothesis to the normalized remaining weights. Convexity then gives $h(\sum_i\theta_iq_i)\le\theta_jh(q_j)+(1-\theta_j)h(y)\le\sum_i\theta_i h(q_i)$. All terms on the right are finite because $h(q_i)\le a_i$ and the codomain excludes $-\infty$. For $x\in P$ and any $\theta\in\Theta_x$, this gives $h(x)\le\sum_i\theta_i a_i$; taking the minimum yields $h(x)\le f_{\rm mix}(x)$. For $x\notin P$, $h(x)\le+\infty=f_{\rm mix}(x)$. Thus $f_{\rm mix}$ is the greatest convex minorant of the data.

The set $C+V$ is convex: for $c_1,c_2\in C$, $v_1,v_2\in V$, and $t\in[0,1]$, $(1-t)(c_1+v_1)+t(c_2+v_2)=((1-t)c_1+tc_2)+((1-t)v_1+tv_2)\in C+V$ by [F5]. To see it is closed, fix $z=(x,r)\notin C+V$ and write $c=(u,a)\in C$. The distance from $z$ to the ray $c+V$ is $\rho_z(c)=\sqrt{\|x-u\|_2^2+\max\{a-r,0\}^2}$: if $r\ge a$ the closest ray point has height $r$, and if $r<a$ it has height $a$. This formula is continuous in $c$ because $\max\{w,0\}=(w+|w|)/2$, and it is positive for every $c\in C$ since $z\notin c+V$. Compactness of $C$ and [F3] give a minimum $\delta>0$; every point of $C+V$ is at distance at least $\delta$ from $z$, so the ball of radius $\delta/2$ about $z$ misses $C+V$.

By [F4] and step 3.1, $f_{\rm mix}$ is convex and lower semicontinuous. It is proper because $P$ is nonempty, each value on $P$ is finite by step 1.1, and it is $+\infty$ outside $P$. Therefore [F6] gives $f_{\rm mix}=f_{\rm mix}^{**}$.

Let $p\in\partial f_{\rm mix}(x)$ and let $\theta$ attain the minimum defining $f_{\rm mix}(x)$. By [F7], $f_{\rm mix}^*(p)=\langle p,x\rangle-f_{\rm mix}(x)$. Also $f_{\rm mix}(q_i)\le a_i$ implies $\langle p,q_i\rangle-a_i\le\langle p,q_i\rangle-f_{\rm mix}(q_i)\le f_{\rm mix}^*(p)$. Since $\langle p,x\rangle-f_{\rm mix}(x)=\sum_i\theta_i(\langle p,q_i\rangle-a_i)$ is a weighted average of terms bounded above by $f_{\rm mix}^*(p)$, each term with $\theta_i>0$ equals that bound, proving the supporting-hyperplane formula.

citations.quote:
Let $s,r\ge1$, let $\nu\in\mathbb R^{s\times r}$ be a stoichiometric matrix (column $k$ gives the signed species-amount change per unit extent of reaction $k$), and let $n^0\in[0,\infty)^s$ be initial species amounts. Extents $\xi\in\mathbb R^r$ are measured in one fixed amount unit, so $n(\xi)=n^0+\nu\xi$ has species amounts in that same unit; $\nu$ is dimensionless. The feasible extent set is the polyhedron

$$\mathcal F=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^r:n^0+\nu\xi\in[0,\infty)^s\}.$$

At $\xi_*\in\mathcal F$, let $J=\{j:n^0_j+(\nu\xi_*)_j=0\}$ be the active species set. Define the Bouligand tangent cone $T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)$ to consist of all $h\in\mathbb R^r$ for which there are $t_k>0$ with $t_k\to0$ and $h_k\to h$ such that $\xi_*+t_kh_k\in\mathcal F$. Then

$$T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)=\{h\in\mathbb R^r:(\nu h)_j\ge0\text{ for every }j\in J\}.$$

If $U\subseteq\mathbb R^r$ is open with $\xi_*\in U$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R$ is differentiable with a local minimum at $\xi_*$ relative to $\mathcal F\cap U$, then $Df(\xi_*)h\ge0$ for every $h\in T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)$. Conversely, if $U$ is convex and $f$ is convex and differentiable on $U$, this directional inequality for every $h\in T_{\mathcal F}(\xi_*)$ implies $f(\xi)\ge f(\xi_*)$ for every $\xi\in\mathcal F\cap U$. Suppose $V\subseteq\mathbb R^s$ is open, $n_*:=n^0+\nu\xi_*\in V$, $\Phi:V\to\mathbb R$ is totally differentiable at $n_*$, and $f(\xi)=\Phi(n^0+\nu\xi)$ near $\xi_*$. For each $j$, let $e_j\in\mathbb R^s$ have coordinate $1$ in position $j$ and $0$ in every other position; define $\mu_j:=D\Phi(n_*)e_j$. Then

$$Df(\xi_*)h=\sum_{j=1}^s\mu_j(\nu h)_j=(\nu^{\mathsf T}\mu)\cdot h.$$

The tangent-cone and optimality claims are mathematical deductions. They do not assert that a particular physical system obeys this model or is at equilibrium.

derivations.claim: The species-amount vector is $n(\xi)=n^0+\nu\xi=(2-2\xi,1-\xi,2\xi)^{\mathsf T}$. Nonnegativity of its third component requires $\xi\ge0$, and nonnegativity of its first two components requires $\xi\le1$; hence the feasible set is exactly $[0,1]$.

The elemental count matrix is $D=\begin{pmatrix}2&0&2\\0&2&1\end{pmatrix}$, with first row counting hydrogen atoms and second row oxygen atoms per molecule. Direct multiplication gives $D\nu=(-4+4,-2+2)^{\mathsf T}=(0,0)^{\mathsf T}$, so every change $n(\xi)-n^0=\nu\xi$ preserves both atom totals.

At $\xi_*=0$, only the water component is zero. Its directional change is $(\nu h)_3=2h$, so [L1] gives $T_{\mathcal F}(0)=\{h:2h\ge0\}=[0,\infty)$. A negative direction is infeasible because it would make the water amount $2\xi$ negative.

For $\Phi(n)=n_3$, the induced function is $f(\xi)=\Phi(n(\xi))=2\xi$. Its derivative at $0$ is $Df(0)h=2h\ge0$ for every feasible tangent $h\ge0$, and $f(\xi)\ge f(0)$ for every $\xi\in[0,1]$. This verifies the boundary first-order condition and minimum directly for this chosen mathematical objective.

citations.quote: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. Suppose every partial derivative $\partial_jf$ exists on a neighbourhood of $a\in U$ and is continuous at $a$. Then $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$, and $Df(a)$ is the linear map with matrix $Jf(a)$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be convex and open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at every point. If $M\ge0$ satisfies $\|Df(z)v\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ for every $z\in U$ and $v\in\mathbb R^m$, then

$$\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

derivations.claim: By openness choose $R>0$ with $\overline B(q_0,2R)\subset U$. Continuity of $X$ and $DX$ at $q_0$ gives finite $M,L\ge0$ bounding $\|X\|$ on $\overline B(q_0,R)$ and $\|DX\|$ on $B(q_0,2R)$. By [F1] $X$ is totally differentiable there, and [F2] applied to the convex ball $B(q_0,2R)$ gives $\|X(u)-X(v)\|\le L\|u-v\|$ for $u,v\in\overline B(q_0,R)$.

Choose $\delta>0$ with $M\delta\le R/2$ and $L\delta<1$, and let $\mathcal C:=\{\gamma\in C([-\delta,\delta],\mathbb R^m):\gamma(t)\in\overline B(q_0,R)\text{ for every }t\}$ with the supremum norm. It is complete: for a supremum-Cauchy sequence $(\gamma_k)$, [F5] gives the pointwise limit $\gamma(t)\in\mathbb R^m$; the supremum-Cauchy estimate, passed to that pointwise limit, gives uniform convergence to $\gamma$. The limit is continuous: given $\varepsilon>0$ and $t_0$, choose $k$ with $\|\gamma_k-\gamma\|_\infty<\varepsilon/3$, then continuity gives $\rho>0$ such that $\|\gamma_k(t)-\gamma_k(t_0)\|<\varepsilon/3$ whenever $|t-t_0|<\rho$; the triangle inequality yields $\|\gamma(t)-\gamma(t_0)\|<\varepsilon$. Also $\gamma(t)\in\overline B(q_0,R)$ for every $t$, since this Euclidean ball is closed and each $\gamma_k(t)$ lies in it. Thus $\gamma\in\mathcal C$. For $p\in\overline B(q_0,R/2)$ define $T_p\gamma(t):=p+\int_0^t X(\gamma(s))\,ds$. The integrand is continuous and hence integrable by [F3]. Then $T_p$ maps $\mathcal C$ into itself, since $\|T_p\gamma(t)-q_0\|\le\|p-q_0\|+M|t|\le R$, and is a contraction with constant at most $L\delta$.

Starting at the constant curve $\gamma_0(t)=p$, iterate $\gamma_{k+1}=T_p\gamma_k$. If $\kappa=L\delta<1$, then $\|\gamma_{k+1}-\gamma_k\|_\infty\le\kappa^k\|\gamma_1-\gamma_0\|_\infty$; the geometric tail bound makes $(\gamma_k)$ uniformly Cauchy. Its limit $\phi(\cdot,p)\in\mathcal C$ is a fixed point by the contraction bound. Any two fixed points have distance at most $\kappa$ times that distance, so they coincide.

For $g(s)=X(\phi(s,p))$, continuity and [F3] make every component Riemann integrable. At an interior $t$, the difference quotient of $\phi(t,p)=p+\int_0^t g(s)\,ds$ differs from $g(t)$ by at most $\sup_{|s-t|\le|h|}\|g(s)-g(t)\|$, which tends to zero by continuity; thus $\partial_t\phi=X(\phi)$. Conversely any $C^1$ solution staying in the ball satisfies the fixed-point equation by [F4], so uniqueness of the fixed point is uniqueness of the IVP.

If $p,p'$ lie in $\overline B(q_0,R/2)$, subtract their fixed-point equations from step 3.1 and take suprema to obtain $\|\phi(\cdot,p)-\phi(\cdot,p')\|_\infty\le\|p-p'\|+L\delta\|\phi(\cdot,p)-\phi(\cdot,p')\|_\infty$. Since $L\delta<1$, division gives the local Lipschitz estimate $(1-L\delta)^{-1}\|p-p'\|$.

Whenever the compositions remain in the chosen ball, both $t\mapsto\phi(t+s,p)$ and $t\mapsto\phi(t,\phi(s,p))$ solve the same IVP at $t=0$, with initial value $\phi(s,p)$. Uniqueness from step 4.1 gives the local flow law; setting $t=-s$ gives the local inverse relation.

citations.quote: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, $m\ge1$, let $X:U\to\mathbb R^m$ have continuous first partial derivatives, and fix $q_0\in U$. There are $r,\delta>0$ and a map $\phi:[-\delta,\delta]\times\overline B(q_0,r/2)\to\overline B(q_0,r)$ such that for each $p\in\overline B(q_0,r/2)$, $t\mapsto\phi(t,p)$ is $C^1$, satisfies $\phi(0,p)=p$ and $\partial_t\phi(t,p)=X(\phi(t,p))$ on $(-\delta,\delta)$, and is the unique such solution that stays in $\overline B(q_0,r)$. The dependence on the initial point is locally Lipschitz, and the local flow law $\phi(t,\phi(s,p))=\phi(t+s,p)$ holds whenever the displayed maps are defined in the chosen neighborhood.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space ([[def-complete-metric-space]])
and let $f : X \to X$ be a contraction with constant $q$, so
$d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$ and $0 \le q < 1$
([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]). Then:

1. There is exactly one $x^{*} \in X$ with $f(x^{*}) = x^{*}$.
2. For every $x_0 \in X$ the sequence of **iterates**, defined by recursion
   ([[thm-recursion]]) by $x_{n+1} := f(x_n)$, converges to $x^{*}$ in $(X,d)$
   ([[def-metric-convergence]]). In particular the limit does not depend on
   $x_0$.
3. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge n$,
   $$d(x_m, x_n) \;\le\; \frac{q^{\,n}\, d(x_1,x_0)}{1-q},$$
   with the integer power of [[def-integer-power]].

Claim 3 is the quantitative form of the argument that proves claims 1 and 2, and
it is recorded in the statement because the error estimates
([[cor-banach-error-estimates]]) are read off from it.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. Suppose every partial derivative $\partial_jf$ exists on a neighbourhood of $a\in U$ and is continuous at $a$. Then $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$, and $Df(a)$ is the linear map with matrix $Jf(a)$.

derivations.claim: For $p$ near $q$ put $\Delta_h(t):=\phi_X^t(p+h)-\phi_X^t(p)$. The integral equations from [F1] and the one-variable fundamental theorem applied to $\theta\mapsto X(\phi_X^s(p)+\theta\Delta_h(s))$ give $$\Delta_h(t)=h+\int_0^t A_h(s)\Delta_h(s)\,ds,\quad A_h(s):=\int_0^1DX(\phi_X^s(p)+\theta\Delta_h(s))\,d\theta.$$ The segments lie in $K$ after shrinking the initial ball and time interval. The local Lipschitz estimate in [F1] gives $\sup_t\|\Delta_h(t)\|=O(\|h\|)$. Uniform continuity of $DX$ on $K$ from [F4] makes $A_h(s)$ converge uniformly to $DX(\phi_X^s(p))$ as $h\to0$.

Let $\mathcal I=[-\delta,\delta]$ and let $\mathcal C_1=C(\mathcal I,M_m(\mathbb R))$ with the supremum operator norm. This space is complete: for a supremum-Cauchy sequence $(J_k)$, each matrix entry at each $s$ is Cauchy because $|A_{ij}|\le\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}$; [F5] applied to the $m^2$ entries gives a pointwise matrix limit $J(s)$, and the uniform Cauchy estimate passed to each entry gives uniform convergence of all entries. Each limit entry is continuous by the $\varepsilon/3$ argument for uniform limits of continuous functions. The finite-coordinate bound $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\sum_{i,j}|A_{ij}|$ then gives uniform operator-norm convergence, so $J\in\mathcal C_1$. The space is nonempty because it contains the constant zero matrix curve. Put $A_0(s):=DX(\phi_X^s(p))$ and define $T(J)(t):=I_m+\int_0^t A_0(s)J(s)\,ds$. It maps $\mathcal C_1$ into itself and is a contraction with constant at most $L\delta<1$. By [F6], it has a unique fixed point $J$. Define $R_h(t):=\Delta_h(t)-J(t)h$. Subtracting the integral equations and writing the integrand difference as $(A_h-A_0)\Delta_h+A_0R_h$ gives $\|R_h\|_\infty\le L\delta\|R_h\|_\infty+\delta\|A_h-A_0\|_\infty\|\Delta_h\|_\infty=o(\|h\|)$, by step 1.1 and uniform continuity of $DX$ on $K$. Thus $D_q\phi_X^t(p)=J(t,p)$. The continuous integrand in the equation for $J$ has average over $[t,t+h]$ tending to its value at $t$: the quotient error is at most $\sup_{|s-t|\le|h|}\|DX(\phi_X^s(p))J(s,p)-DX(\phi_X^t(p))J(t,p)\|$, which tends to zero. Thus $\partial_tJ=DX(\phi_X^t(p))J$ and $J(0,p)=I_m$.

Write $J_h(s)=D_q\phi_X^s(p+h)$ and $J_0(s)=D_q\phi_X^s(p)$. Subtracting their integral equations gives $J_h-J_0=\int_0^t A_0(J_h-J_0)\,ds+\int_0^t(A_h-A_0)J_h\,ds$, where $A_h=DX(\phi_h)$, $A_0=DX(\phi_0)$, $\phi_h=\phi_X^s(p+h)$, and $\phi_0=\phi_X^s(p)$. The line-segment chain rule and Newton–Leibniz supplier claims in [F2]–[F3], applied entrywise to $DX$ along the segment from $\phi_0$ to $\phi_h$, give the exact formula $A_h-A_0=\int_0^1D^2X(\phi_0+\theta(\phi_h-\phi_0))[\phi_h-\phi_0,\cdot]\,d\theta$ and therefore $\|A_h-A_0\|_\infty\le M_2\|\phi_h-\phi_0\|_\infty$. By [F1], $\|\phi_h-\phi_0\|_\infty=O(\|h\|)$; the integral equation gives $\|J_h\|_\infty\le(1-L\delta)^{-1}$. Absorbing the first integral using $L\delta<1$ yields $J_h-J_0=O(\|h\|)$ uniformly in time. Uniform continuity of $D^2X$ on $K$, the same line-segment formula, and $\phi_h-\phi_0=J_0h+o(\|h\|)$ from step 2.1 now give $A_h-A_0=D^2X(\phi_0)[J_0h,\cdot]+o(\|h\|)$ uniformly, and hence $(A_h-A_0)J_h=D^2X(\phi_0)[J_0h,J_0(\cdot)]+o(\|h\|)$. For each base point $p$, define $\mathcal C_2=C(\mathcal I,\operatorname{Bil}(\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^m,\mathbb R^m))$ with the supremum bilinear-operator norm. The coordinatewise completeness proof of step 2.1 applies with $m^3$ coefficients, so $\mathcal C_2$ is complete; it is nonempty because it contains the zero bilinear-map curve. The map $(\mathcal T K)(t)[u,v]:=\int_0^t\big(A_0(s)K(s)[u,v]+D^2X(\phi_0(s))[J_0(s)u,J_0(s)v]\big)\,ds$ is a contraction with constant at most $L\delta$ on $\mathcal C_2$. By [F6] it has a unique fixed point $K_p$. Subtracting its equation evaluated at $(h,v)$ from the equation for $J_h-J_0$ gives $R_h:=J_h-J_0-K_p[h,\cdot]$ with $\|R_h\|_\infty\le L\delta\|R_h\|_\infty+o(\|h\|)$, so $R_h=o(\|h\|)$. Therefore $D_pJ[h](v)=K_p[h,v]$, and $K_p$ is the second derivative $D_q^2\phi_X$. Its equation makes it bilinear. The coefficients, forcing, $\phi_p$, and $J_p$ vary continuously in $p$ uniformly for $s\in\mathcal I$; for fixed-point maps $T_p$ with contraction constant $L\delta$, $\|K_p-K_{p'}\|_\infty\le(1-L\delta)^{-1}\|T_p(K_{p'})-T_{p'}(K_{p'})\|_\infty\to0$. The integral equation gives continuity in $t$ as well. Thus the second derivatives in $q$ are continuous.

Let $V(t):=Y(\phi_X^t(q))$ and $W(t):=D_q\phi_X^t(q)Y(q)$. By [F2] and the variational equation, $V'=DY(\phi_X^t)X(\phi_X^t)$ and $W'=DX(\phi_X^t)W$. The identity $[X,Y]=0$ makes $V$ solve this same linear equation with $V(0)=W(0)=Y(q)$; uniqueness from the contraction argument gives $D_q\phi_X^t(q)Y(q)=Y(\phi_X^t(q))$.

On the open interior of the chosen time and initial-point neighborhood, step 2.1 gives $D_q\phi_X=J$ and $\partial_tJ=DX(\phi_X)J$, while step 3.1 gives the continuous second derivative $D_qJ=K$. The chain rule [F2] applied to $\partial_t\phi_X=X(\phi_X)$ gives $\partial_{q_i}\partial_t\phi_X=DX(\phi_X)Je_i$, and the variational equation gives $\partial_t\partial_{q_i}\phi_X=DX(\phi_X)Je_i$; also $\partial_t^2\phi_X=DX(\phi_X)X(\phi_X)$. Hence all first- and second-order coordinate partial derivatives of $\phi_X$ exist and are continuous there. Apply [F7] pointwise first to $\phi_X$ and then to its first-derivative map: its Jacobian is the matrix of first partials, and the Jacobian of that map is the continuous array of second partials. Thus $\phi_X$ is jointly $C^2$.

For fixed $t$, the curve $s\mapsto\phi_X^t(\phi_Y^s(q))$ has derivative $D\phi_X^t\,Y(\phi_Y^s(q))=Y(\phi_X^t(\phi_Y^s(q))$ by step 3.2, and starts at $\phi_X^t(q)$. It is therefore the $Y$-flow from that initial point; IVP uniqueness from [F1] yields $\phi_X^t\phi_Y^s(q)=\phi_Y^s\phi_X^t(q)$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ be open, $n\ge1$, with coordinates $(x_1,\ldots,x_n,z)$. For $k\in\{1,2\}$, a $C^k$ one-form on $U$ is a field of linear functionals on tangent vectors of the form $\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i(x,z)\,dx_i+b(x,z)\,dz$, where every coefficient is $k$ times continuously differentiable. At $q\in U$, it acts by $\omega_q(u_1,\ldots,u_n,w)=\sum_i a_i(q)u_i+b(q)w$. It is nonsingular on $U$ when $\omega_q\ne0$ for every $q$; then $H_q:=\ker\omega_q$ is an $n$-dimensional subspace of $T_qU\cong\mathbb R^{n+1}$.

For a $C^1$ scalar function $S:W\to\mathbb R$ on an open $W\subseteq U$, its differential is the one-form defined by

$$dS_q(v):=DS(q)v=\sum_{i=1}^n\partial_{x_i}S(q)u_i+\partial_zS(q)w,\qquad v=(u_1,\ldots,u_n,w)\in T_qW.$$

In particular, if $S\in C^2(W)$, then $dS$ is a $C^1$ one-form.

For one-forms $\alpha,\beta$, their exterior product is the alternating two-form $(\alpha\wedge\beta)(u,v)=\alpha(u)\beta(v)-\alpha(v)\beta(u)$. For a one-form $\alpha$ and a two-form $\sigma$, $(\alpha\wedge\sigma)(u,v,w)=\alpha(u)\sigma(v,w)-\alpha(v)\sigma(u,w)+\alpha(w)\sigma(u,v)$. For a $C^1$ one-form $\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\,dx_i+b\,dz$, its exterior derivative is the continuous two-form

$$d\omega=\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}(\partial_i a_j-\partial_j a_i)\,dx_i\wedge dx_j+\sum_{i=1}^n(\partial_i b-\partial_z a_i)\,dx_i\wedge dz.$$

When $\omega$ is $C^2$, the coefficients of $d\omega$ are $C^1$.

For a $C^2$ one-form on this page, the codimension-one Pfaff condition means the pointwise equation $\omega\wedge d\omega=0$.

A piecewise-$C^1$ path is a continuous $\gamma:[s_0,s_1]\to U$ with $s_0\le s_1$ and admitting a finite partition on each closed subinterval of which it is $C^1$. It is $\omega$-horizontal when $\omega_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t))=0$ on the interior of each such subinterval. Endpoints where a derivative is one-sided are included by continuity. For an open $V\subseteq U$, $p$ is horizontally reachable from $q$ within $V$ if a horizontal path in $V$ joins $q$ to $p$. Both signs of time and finite concatenations are allowed by this definition.

On a neighborhood $W$, an integrating factor for $\omega$ is a nowhere-zero $\mu\in C^1(W)$ for which $\mu\omega=dS$ for some $S\in C^2(W)$ with $dS$ nowhere zero. This definition is local; it asserts neither a global potential on $U$ nor a physical identification or calibration of $S$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

Fix $q\in U$ and distinct coordinates $i,j$. Choose $h,k>0$ small enough that the coordinate rectangle from $q$ to $q+he_i+ke_j$ lies in $U$, and set $\Delta=S(q+he_i+ke_j)-S(q+he_i)-S(q+ke_j)+S(q)$. By [F4] the second partials are uniformly continuous on the chosen closed rectangle. Applying [F2] to coordinate segments and [F3] to their continuous derivatives, Newton–Leibniz gives
$$\Delta=\int_0^h\!\int_0^k S_{ij}(q+se_i+te_j)\,dt\,ds=\int_0^k\!\int_0^h S_{ji}(q+se_i+te_j)\,ds\,dt.$$
Each equality follows by taking the two endpoint differences in the outer coordinate and then applying Newton–Leibniz to the inner difference; both integrands are continuous by $S\in C^2$.

Divide both expressions in step 1.1 by $hk$ and let $h,k\downarrow0$. Continuity of $S_{ij}$ and $S_{ji}$ makes each average tend to its value at $q$, so $S_{ij}(q)=S_{ji}(q)$. Since $q,i,j$ were arbitrary, the coordinate formula in [F1] gives $d(dS)=0$.

Put $\lambda:=1/\mu\in C^1(U)$. Then $\omega=\lambda dS$. Expanding the coordinate derivative by the product rule and using step 2.1 yields $d\omega=d\lambda\wedge dS$. Therefore $\omega\wedge d\omega=\lambda\,dS\wedge d\lambda\wedge dS=0$, because the alternating product vanishes when the same one-form $dS$ occurs twice.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, $m\ge1$, let $X:U\to\mathbb R^m$ have continuous first partial derivatives, and fix $q_0\in U$. For two such fields define their bracket by $[X,Y](q):=DY(q)X(q)-DX(q)Y(q)$. If $[X,Y]=0$ on a neighborhood and all local maps stay there, then $D_q\phi_X^t(q)Y(q)=Y(\phi_X^t(q))$ and their local flows commute: $\phi_X^t\circ\phi_Y^s=\phi_Y^s\circ\phi_X^t$ whenever both sides are defined.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $1\le q\le n$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^q$ be $C^1$ in the sense of [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]. Suppose $F(x_*)=0$ and some $q\times q$ minor of the derivative matrix $DF(x_*)$ is invertible. This nonsingular-minor hypothesis is the explicit full-row-rank condition used here. If $q<n$, then after permuting coordinates $x=(u,v)\in\mathbb R^{n-q}\times\mathbb R^q$, there are open neighborhoods $P$ of $u_*$ and $Q$ of $v_*$ and a unique $C^1$ map $\varphi:P\to Q$ such that

$$F(u,v)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v=\varphi(u)\qquad((u,v)\in P\times Q).$$

Its derivative is

$$D\varphi(u)=-D_vF(u,\varphi(u))^{-1}D_uF(u,\varphi(u)).$$

Thus the local zero set is a graph over $n-q$ free coordinates. If $q=n$, the zero is locally isolated, so the local graph dimension is zero. Here “local graph dimension $k$” means a local graph parameterized by an open subset of $\mathbb R^k$, with a singleton counted as dimension zero.

derivations.claim: Since $\omega_{q_0}\ne0$, one coordinate coefficient is nonzero at $q_0$; relabel that coordinate as $z$ and shrink the neighborhood so $b\ne0$. Put $c_i:=-a_i/b$ and $X_i:=\partial_{x_i}+c_i\partial_z$. Then $X_i\in C^2$, $\omega(X_i)=a_i+bc_i=0$, and the $X_i$ are a basis of $\ker\omega$ because their first $n$ components form the standard basis.

Define $[X,Y]:=DY\,X-DX\,Y$. Coordinate expansion of the displayed formula for $d\omega$ gives $d\omega(X,Y)=X[\omega(Y)]-Y[\omega(X)]-\omega([X,Y])$. Thus for horizontal fields $d\omega(X_i,X_j)=-\omega([X_i,X_j])$. Also $[X_i,X_j]$ has zero $x$-components, hence is vertical. Evaluating the three-form on $(\partial_z,X_i,X_j)$ gives $(\omega\wedge d\omega)(\partial_z,X_i,X_j)=b\,d\omega(X_i,X_j)$. Under (i), $d\omega(X_i,X_j)=0$; then $\omega([X_i,X_j])=0$, and a vertical vector $v\partial_z$ has $\omega(v\partial_z)=vb$, so $[X_i,X_j]=0$.

By [F2]–[F3] and step 1.2, the fields $X_i$ have commuting local $C^2$ flows $\phi_i^t$. Define $\Phi(x,\eta):=\phi_n^{x_n}\circ\cdots\circ\phi_1^{x_1}(0,\eta)$ for $(x,\eta)$ near $(0,z_0)$. Each $X_i$ changes only $x_i$, at rate one, so the first $n$ coordinates of $\Phi(x,\eta)$ are exactly $x$. Commutation and the transported-field identity in [F3] give $\partial_{x_i}\Phi=X_i(\Phi)$. At $(0,z_0)$ the columns of $D\Phi$ are $X_1,\ldots,X_n,\partial_z$; their first $n$ components form $I_n$ and the last column is $\partial_z$, so $D\Phi$ is invertible.

Let $N=n+1$. On an open product neighborhood of $(u_0,y_0)=((0,z_0),(0,z_0))$ where $\Phi$ is defined, set $H(u,y):=\Phi(u)-y$. Then $H(u_0,y_0)=0$ and its $u$-derivative $D_uH=D\Phi(u_0)$ is invertible. Apply [L1] with ambient dimension $2N$ and target dimension $N$, permuting the input coordinates to $(y,u)$ so the $y$ block is free and the solved $u$ block has the invertible minor: conditionally, the zero set is the graph of a unique local $C^1$ map $G(y)$, so $\Phi(G(y))=y$. Since $\Phi$ is $C^2$, differentiating this identity by [F5] gives $D\Phi(G(y))DG(y)=I$ and hence $DG(y)=(D\Phi(G(y)))^{-1}$. The right side is $C^1$ (matrix inverse entries are cofactors divided by the nonzero determinant), so $G$ is $C^2$.

Let $S(x,z)$ be the last coordinate $\eta$ of $G(x,z)$. Then $S\in C^2$, $S(\Phi(x,\eta))=\eta$, and $S_z(0,z_0)=1$; after shrinking, $S_z\ne0$. Differentiating along $X_i$ gives $S_{x_i}+c_iS_z=0$, so $dS=S_z(dz-\sum_i c_i dx_i)=(S_z/b)\omega$. Thus $\mu:=S_z/b$ is $C^1$ and nowhere zero. This proves (ii), conditionally on [L1].
Conversely, if (ii) holds, [F4] gives $\omega\wedge d\omega=0$ on that neighborhood, proving (i).

boundaries.evidence: Statement fixes q_0 in the open neighborhood and n>=1, with a nonzero one-form there. Thus its local integration argument does not start from an empty neighborhood or a missing base point.

case_scope.source_excerpt: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$, $n\ge1$, be open and let $\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i dx_i+b dz$ be a $C^2$ one-form with $\omega_{q_0}\ne0$ at $q_0\in U$. Relabel coordinates so one coefficient $b$ is nonzero at $q_0$ and shrink to a neighborhood where it stays nonzero. The following conditions, both local at $q_0$, are equivalent: (i) there is a neighborhood $U_0$ of $q_0$ on which $\omega\wedge d\omega=0$; (ii) there is a neighborhood $W$ of $q_0$ and $\mu\in C^1(W)$ nowhere zero and $S\in C^2(W)$ with $dS=\mu\omega$ on $W$. The theorem gives no global exactness or thermodynamic calibration.

If the initially named coefficient b(q0) vanishes, a finite coordinate relabel selects a nonzero component; if omega(q0)=0 the theorem excludes the point, step 1.1.

Only finite coordinate choices and a deterministic flow composition are used in steps 1.1 and 2.1; the separate local-rank input is conditional at step 3.1.
The Pfaff condition constructs mu and S conditionally on the rank carrier through steps 1.1–4.1.
An exact nonzero multiple implies the Pfaff condition by the local exactness lemma in step 5.1.

When $\omega$ is $C^2$, the coefficients of $d\omega$ are $C^1$.

For a $C^2$ one-form on this page, the codimension-one Pfaff condition means the pointwise equation $\omega\wedge d\omega=0$.

A piecewise-$C^1$ path is a continuous $\gamma:[s_0,s_1]\to U$ with $s_0\le s_1$ and admitting a finite partition on each closed subinterval of which it is $C^1$. It is $\omega$-horizontal when $\omega_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t))=0$ on the interior of each such subinterval. Endpoints where a derivative is one-sided are included by continuity. For an open $V\subseteq U$, $p$ is horizontally reachable from $q$ within $V$ if a horizontal path in $V$ joins $q$ to $p$. Both signs of time and finite concatenations are allowed by this definition.

On a neighborhood $W$, an integrating factor for $\omega$ is a nowhere-zero $\mu\in C^1(W)$ for which $\mu\omega=dS$ for some $S\in C^2(W)$ with $dS$ nowhere zero. This definition is local; it asserts neither a global potential on $U$ nor a physical identification or calibration of $S$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, $m\ge1$, let $X:U\to\mathbb R^m$ have continuous first partial derivatives, and fix $q_0\in U$. There are $r,\delta>0$ and a map $\phi:[-\delta,\delta]\times\overline B(q_0,r/2)\to\overline B(q_0,r)$ such that for each $p\in\overline B(q_0,r/2)$, $t\mapsto\phi(t,p)$ is $C^1$, satisfies $\phi(0,p)=p$ and $\partial_t\phi(t,p)=X(\phi(t,p))$ on $(-\delta,\delta)$, and is the unique such solution that stays in $\overline B(q_0,r)$. The dependence on the initial point is locally Lipschitz, and the local flow law $\phi(t,\phi(s,p))=\phi(t+s,p)$ holds whenever the displayed maps are defined in the chosen neighborhood.

Let $X$ be a $C^2$ vector field on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, where $C^2$ means that total derivatives through order two exist and are continuous. Its local flow $\phi_X^t(q)$ from [[lem-tdmath-local-contraction-flow]] is $C^2$ jointly in $(t,q)$, and $J(t,q):=D_q\phi_X^t(q)$ satisfies $\partial_tJ=DX(\phi_X^t(q))J$ and $J(0,q)=I$. For two such fields define their bracket by $[X,Y](q):=DY(q)X(q)-DX(q)Y(q)$. If $[X,Y]=0$ on a neighborhood and all local maps stay there, then $D_q\phi_X^t(q)Y(q)=Y(\phi_X^t(q))$ and their local flows commute: $\phi_X^t\circ\phi_Y^s=\phi_Y^s\circ\phi_X^t$ whenever both sides are defined.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$, $n\ge1$, be open and let $\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i dx_i+b dz$ be a $C^2$ one-form with $\omega_{q_0}\ne0$ at $q_0\in U$. Relabel coordinates so one coefficient $b$ is nonzero at $q_0$ and shrink to a neighborhood where it stays nonzero. The following conditions, both local at $q_0$, are equivalent: (i) there is a neighborhood $U_0$ of $q_0$ on which $\omega\wedge d\omega=0$; (ii) there is a neighborhood $W$ of $q_0$ and $\mu\in C^1(W)$ nowhere zero and $S\in C^2(W)$ with $dS=\mu\omega$ on $W$. The theorem gives no global exactness or thermodynamic calibration.

Let $1\le q\le n$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^q$ be $C^1$ in the sense of [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]. Suppose $F(x_*)=0$ and some $q\times q$ minor of the derivative matrix $DF(x_*)$ is invertible. This nonsingular-minor hypothesis is the explicit full-row-rank condition used here. If $q<n$, then after permuting coordinates $x=(u,v)\in\mathbb R^{n-q}\times\mathbb R^q$, there are open neighborhoods $P$ of $u_*$ and $Q$ of $v_*$ and a unique $C^1$ map $\varphi:P\to Q$ such that

$$F(u,v)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v=\varphi(u)\qquad((u,v)\in P\times Q).$$

Its derivative is

$$D\varphi(u)=-D_vF(u,\varphi(u))^{-1}D_uF(u,\varphi(u)).$$

Thus the local zero set is a graph over $n-q$ free coordinates. If $q=n$, the zero is locally isolated, so the local graph dimension is zero. Here “local graph dimension $k$” means a local graph parameterized by an open subset of $\mathbb R^k$, with a singleton counted as dimension zero.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$, $n\ge1$, be open, and let $\omega$ be a nowhere-zero $C^2$ one-form, with the horizontal paths of [[def-tdmath-one-form-and-horizontal-path]]. Assume that every point has a neighborhood $W$ with $S\in C^2(W)$ and nowhere-zero $\mu\in C^1(W)$ satisfying $dS=\mu\omega$. For every $q\in U$, its horizontal reachability class in $U$ is contained in a countable union of compact subsets of $U$ with empty interior. Consequently every nonempty open $V\subseteq U$ contains a point not horizontally reachable from $q$ by any horizontal path in $U$. In particular, if $q\in V$, that point is not reachable by a path contained in $V$. No global first integral or choice axiom is assumed.

Let $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. Then $E$ is connected ([[def-connected-r]]) if and
only if $E$ is **order-convex** ([[def-interval]]), that is, if and only if

$$x, z \in E \text{ and } x \le w \le z \;\Longrightarrow\; w \in E .$$

**On the word "interval".** Order-convexity is exactly the defining property
that [[def-interval]] proves for each of its nine forms, and in that sense the
theorem says that the connected subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ are the intervals. The
converse classification, that every order-convex subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is empty
or one of the nine forms, is true and is explicitly **not proved anywhere in
this library**; [[def-interval]] records that omission in its own remarks. So
the statement proved below is the equivalence with order-convexity, and the
phrase "is an interval" is to be read as "is order-convex" throughout this page.

Starting at $r$, compose this flow with those of $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ to obtain a $C^2$ endpoint map $\Psi_r$ near the zero duration vector. Then $\Psi_r(0)=r$ and its derivative has the independent columns $X_1(r),\ldots,X_n(r),Y_t(r)$. Conditionally, some open neighborhood $O_r\subseteq B$ of $r$ consists of endpoints $\Psi_r(s(p))$, all reachable from $r$ by horizontal paths inside $B$. Reachability inside $B$ is an equivalence relation: constant paths give reflexivity, path reversal gives symmetry, and finite concatenation gives transitivity. Every equivalence class is open in $B$, since each of its points $r$ has $O_r$ in that same class. If there were more than one class, one class and the union of all other classes would be disjoint nonempty open subsets covering $B$. Write $B=B(c,R)$. It is convex: for $x,y\in B$ and $0\le\lambda\le1$, the triangle inequality gives $\|(1-\lambda)x+\lambda y-c\|\le(1-\lambda)\|x-c\|+\lambda\|y-c\|<R$. Choose a point in each set and join them by their straight segment, which lies in $B$ by this calculation; the preimages of the class and its complement would separate $[0,1]$ into two nonempty relatively open sets, contradicting [F9]. Thus every bracket $[X_i,X_j]$ vanishes by the contradiction at step 4.1. derivations.claim: On $\mathbb R^3$ with coordinates $(x,y,z)$ take $\omega=dz-y\,dx$. It is smooth and nowhere zero because the $dz$ coefficient is $1$.
Its exterior derivative is $d\omega=dx\wedge dy$, so $\omega\wedge d\omega=(dz-y\,dx)\wedge dx\wedge dy=dz\wedge dx\wedge dy$, a nonzero coordinate volume form.

If a local $\mu,S$ as in the refuted claim existed on any open neighborhood, [F2] would force $\omega\wedge d\omega=0$ there, contradicting step 2.1 at every point. Therefore no such local exact multiple exists.

Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^n$ be piecewise-$C^1$. If $a=b$, define both line integrals below to be $0$. If $a<b$, choose an admissible partition $a=t_0<\cdots<t_m=b$ and a continuous derivative extension $v_i$ on each piece. Let $f$ be a continuous scalar field and $F$ a continuous vector field on a set containing the trace of $\gamma$. The **scalar line integral with respect to arc length** and the **vector-field line integral** are

$$\int_\gamma f\,ds:=\sum_{i<m}\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}f(\gamma(t))\lVert v_i(t)\rVert_2\,dt,$$

$$\int_\gamma F\cdot d\mathbf r:=\sum_{i<m}\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}\langle F(\gamma(t)),v_i(t)\rangle\,dt,$$

where the inner product is [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. The summands exist by [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]. Independence of the admissible partition is proved in [[lem-line-integrals-are-independent-of-the-piecewise-c1-partition]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $\phi:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$, and let $\gamma:[a,b]\to U$ be piecewise-$C^1$. Then

$$\int_\gamma\nabla\phi\cdot d\mathbf r=\phi(\gamma(b))-\phi(\gamma(a)).$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

derivations.claim: Let $D=\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}$ and $\omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy$ with $P(x,y)=-y/(x^2+y^2)$ and $Q(x,y)=x/(x^2+y^2)$. The domain $D$ is open since each nonzero point has a ball avoiding the origin, and the coefficients are smooth with $(P,Q)\ne(0,0)$ at every point. It is path-connected: if the segment joining $p,q\in D$ avoids $0$, use that segment; if it contains $0$, then $p,q,0$ are collinear, and a nonzero vector $r$ perpendicular to $p$ makes both segments $[p,r]$ and $[r,q]$ avoid $0$.
Writing $r^2=x^2+y^2$, direct differentiation gives $\partial_xQ=(y^2-x^2)/r^4=\partial_yP$, so $d\omega=(\partial_xQ-\partial_yP)dx\wedge dy=0$ on $D$.

The unit circle $\gamma(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)$, $0\le t\le2\pi$, lies in the domain and uses the form defined in step 1.1. Along it $(P,Q)=(-\sin t,\cos t)=\gamma'(t)$, hence [F2] gives $\int_\gamma\omega=\int_0^{2\pi}1\,dt=2\pi$ by [F4].

The closedness is proved in step 2.1. If $\omega=dS$ globally on $D$, then $F=\nabla S$ for the corresponding vector field, and [F3] would give $\int_\gamma\omega=S(\gamma(2\pi))-S(\gamma(0))=0$, contradicting step 2.2. Thus $\omega$ is closed but not globally exact. This does not assert that every possible global integrating factor is absent.
