$$dS_q(v):=DS(q)v=\sum_{i=1}^n\partial_{x_i}S(q)u_i+\partial_zS(q)w,\qquad v=(u_1,\ldots,u_n,w)\in T_qW.$$

In particular, if $S\in C^2(W)$, then $dS$ is a $C^1$ one-form.

For one-forms $\alpha,\beta$, their exterior product is the alternating two-form $(\alpha\wedge\beta)(u,v)=\alpha(u)\beta(v)-\alpha(v)\beta(u)$. For a one-form $\alpha$ and a two-form $\sigma$, $(\alpha\wedge\sigma)(u,v,w)=\alpha(u)\sigma(v,w)-\alpha(v)\sigma(u,w)+\alpha(w)\sigma(u,v)$. For a $C^1$ one-form $\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\,dx_i+b\,dz$, its exterior derivative is the continuous two-form

$$d\omega=\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}(\partial_i a_j-\partial_j a_i)\,dx_i\wedge dx_j+\sum_{i=1}^n(\partial_i b-\partial_z a_i)\,dx_i\wedge dz.$$

When $\omega$ is $C^2$, the coefficients of $d\omega$ are $C^1$.

For a $C^2$ one-form on this page, the codimension-one Pfaff condition means the pointwise equation $\omega\wedge d\omega=0$.

A piecewise-$C^1$ path is a continuous $\gamma:[s_0,s_1]\to U$ with $s_0\le s_1$ and admitting a finite partition on each closed subinterval of which it is $C^1$. It is $\omega$-horizontal when $\omega_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t))=0$ on the interior of each such subinterval. Endpoints where a derivative is one-sided are included by continuity. For an open $V\subseteq U$, $p$ is horizontally reachable from $q$ within $V$ if a horizontal path in $V$ joins $q$ to $p$. Both signs of time and finite concatenations are allowed by this definition.

On a neighborhood $W$, an integrating factor for $\omega$ is a nowhere-zero $\mu\in C^1(W)$ for which $\mu\omega=dS$ for some $S\in C^2(W)$ with $dS$ nowhere zero. This definition is local; it asserts neither a global potential on $U$ nor a physical identification or calibration of $S$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, $m\ge1$, let $X:U\to\mathbb R^m$ have continuous first partial derivatives, and fix $q_0\in U$. There are $r,\delta>0$ and a map $\phi:[-\delta,\delta]\times\overline B(q_0,r/2)\to\overline B(q_0,r)$ such that for each $p\in\overline B(q_0,r/2)$, $t\mapsto\phi(t,p)$ is $C^1$, satisfies $\phi(0,p)=p$ and $\partial_t\phi(t,p)=X(\phi(t,p))$ on $(-\delta,\delta)$, and is the unique such solution that stays in $\overline B(q_0,r)$. The dependence on the initial point is locally Lipschitz, and the local flow law $\phi(t,\phi(s,p))=\phi(t+s,p)$ holds whenever the displayed maps are defined in the chosen neighborhood.

Let $X$ be a $C^2$ vector field on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, where $C^2$ means that total derivatives through order two exist and are continuous. Its local flow $\phi_X^t(q)$ from [[lem-tdmath-local-contraction-flow]] is $C^2$ jointly in $(t,q)$, and $J(t,q):=D_q\phi_X^t(q)$ satisfies $\partial_tJ=DX(\phi_X^t(q))J$ and $J(0,q)=I$. For two such fields define their bracket by $[X,Y](q):=DY(q)X(q)-DX(q)Y(q)$. If $[X,Y]=0$ on a neighborhood and all local maps stay there, then $D_q\phi_X^t(q)Y(q)=Y(\phi_X^t(q))$ and their local flows commute: $\phi_X^t\circ\phi_Y^s=\phi_Y^s\circ\phi_X^t$ whenever both sides are defined.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $1\le q\le n$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^q$ be $C^1$ in the sense of [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]. Suppose $F(x_*)=0$ and some $q\times q$ minor of the derivative matrix $DF(x_*)$ is invertible. This nonsingular-minor hypothesis is the explicit full-row-rank condition used here. If $q<n$, then after permuting coordinates $x=(u,v)\in\mathbb R^{n-q}\times\mathbb R^q$, there are open neighborhoods $P$ of $u_*$ and $Q$ of $v_*$ and a unique $C^1$ map $\varphi:P\to Q$ such that

$$F(u,v)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v=\varphi(u)\qquad((u,v)\in P\times Q).$$

Its derivative is

$$D\varphi(u)=-D_vF(u,\varphi(u))^{-1}D_uF(u,\varphi(u)).$$

Thus the local zero set is a graph over $n-q$ free coordinates. If $q=n$, the zero is locally isolated, so the local graph dimension is zero. Here “local graph dimension $k$” means a local graph parameterized by an open subset of $\mathbb R^k$, with a singleton counted as dimension zero.

Let $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. Then $E$ is connected ([[def-connected-r]]) if and
only if $E$ is **order-convex** ([[def-interval]]), that is, if and only if

$$x, z \in E \text{ and } x \le w \le z \;\Longrightarrow\; w \in E .$$

**On the word "interval".** Order-convexity is exactly the defining property
that [[def-interval]] proves for each of its nine forms, and in that sense the
theorem says that the connected subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ are the intervals. The
converse classification, that every order-convex subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is empty
or one of the nine forms, is true and is explicitly **not proved anywhere in
this library**; [[def-interval]] records that omission in its own remarks. So
the statement proved below is the equivalence with order-convexity, and the
phrase "is an interval" is to be read as "is order-convex" throughout this page.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

Write $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the image of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$
under the canonical embedding $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), the
set usually written $\mathbb{Q}$ once the identification is made, and put
$X := \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the irrationals. Then:

1. $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$, that is,
   $\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}} = \mathbb{R}$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]);
2. $X$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$;
3. every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable
   ([[def-countable]]).

Claim 2 is not a symmetry of claim 1: the rationals are dense because they are
*constructed* to approximate, whereas the irrationals are dense because there are
too many points in any interval for a countable set to exhaust it, which is why
claim 3 is proved alongside and used for it.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then:

1. If $(X,d_X)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]), the image
   $f[X] \subseteq Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$.
2. More generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$, then $f[K]$ is
   a compact subset of $Y$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $K \subseteq X$ be a
compact subset ([[def-metric-compactness]]). Then $K$ is closed in $X$
([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

No choice principle is used: both covers below are given by a rule, and the
indexed form of [[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]] returns indices rather than
sets.

**The converse is false in general.** A closed and bounded subset of an arbitrary
metric space need not be compact
([[fs-closed-and-bounded-implies-compact-in-every-metric-space]]); it is exactly
in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that the converse holds ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

Let $(N,0,\sigma)$ be a Peano system ([[def-peano-system]]), in particular the natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]). For any set $A$, any element $a \in A$, and any function $f : A \to A$, there is a unique function $g : N \to A$ such that $g(0) = a$ and $g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n))$ for all $n \in N$.
Every nonempty subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has a least element: there is $\ell \in S$ with $\ell \le s$ for all $s \in S$.

derivations.claim: Use the local first integrals in the Statement. Write $\omega=\sum_{j=1}^{n+1}\omega_j dx_j$ in the fixed Euclidean coordinates and set $w=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_{n+1})$ and $Z_j=e_j-(\omega_j/|w|^2)w$. These globally defined $C^2$ vector fields are horizontal and span $\ker\omega$ at each point, since their matrix is the orthogonal projection onto that kernel. On every neighborhood supplied by the hypothesis, $dS=\mu\omega$ has nonzero derivative, and each $Z_j$-flow preserves $S$ as long as its trajectory remains there, by [F3]. Its derivative therefore preserves horizontal tangent vectors there: differentiating $S(\phi_j^t(x))=S(x)$ gives $dS_{\phi_j^t(x)}D\phi_j^t(x)v=dS_xv=0$ for horizontal $v$. The compact image of any finite flow trajectory has a finite subcover by such neighborhoods; a sufficiently fine finite subdivision of its compact time interval puts each subtrajectory in one of them. This follows directly from compactness: otherwise shrinking subintervals failing the subdivision would have a limiting time whose neighborhood contains them. Composing the local derivative identities obtains preservation over the full duration. Local flow uniqueness makes these continuations consistent, and [F2] gives $C^2$ dependence on durations and initial points wherever the finite composition is defined.

Fix $q\in U$ and a neighborhood $W$ with $dS=\mu\omega$ as in the hypothesis. Since $dS_q=\mu(q)\omega_q\ne0$, apply [L1] to $x\mapsto S(x)-S(q)$ with ambient dimension $n+1$ and target dimension $1$; after choosing the solved coordinate, its zero set is a local $C^1$ graph plaque $P$ through $q$, parameterized by its $n$ free coordinates. Let $\pi$ be projection to those free coordinates. Choose $n$ of the fields $Z_j$ that form a basis of $\ker\omega_q=\ker dS_q$, and for $s=(s_1,\ldots,s_n)$ near $0$ let $E(s)$ be the endpoint at $q$ of the successive local flows of these fields for durations $s_1,\ldots,s_n$. Shrink the open duration domain $D\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ so all flow segments stay in $W$. Step 1.1 shows that each flow preserves $S$, so $E(D)\subseteq P$; moreover $DE(0)$ has the chosen basis as its columns. The differential $D(\pi\circ E)(0)$ is therefore an invertible $n\times n$ matrix, because $D\pi_q$ is an isomorphism from the tangent space of the graph plaque to its free-coordinate space. Choose an open neighborhood $Y\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of $y_0=\pi(q)$ and shrink $D$ so that the target-augmented map $H:D\times Y\to\mathbb R^n$, $H(s,y):=\pi(E(s))-y$, is defined. It satisfies $H(0,y_0)=0$ and its solved block $D_sH(0,y_0)=D(\pi\circ E)(0)$ is invertible. Apply [L1] with ambient dimension $2n$ and target dimension $n<2n$, permuting inputs to $(y,s)$ so $y$ is free and $s$ is solved. For every $y$ near $y_0$ this gives $s(y)$ with $\pi(E(s(y)))=y$; uniqueness of the graph plaque then says the endpoints $E(s(y))$ fill a relative neighborhood of $q$ in $P$. Each is reachable by a finite word of horizontal flows inside $W$. Conversely, a horizontal path preserves the local $S$ on each short subarc in a first-integral neighborhood by [F3]. Thus near each parameter value its image lies in the relative plaque neighborhood just shown to be reachable by such a finite word. The finite-word orbits are equivalence classes by flow reversal and concatenation, so their preimages along the path are relatively open in its interval domain. By [F4], connectedness of that interval forces one class. Hence every point horizontally reachable from $q$ lies in its finite-word orbit; the reverse inclusion follows because every word is a horizontal concatenation.

For a fixed finite word $\alpha$ of length $m\ge1$, write $F_\alpha:O_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^m\to U$ for its endpoint map from $q$, on the open set of admissible duration tuples. Each duration derivative is a field vector transported by the later flows and is horizontal by step 1.1. Near any $s\in O_\alpha$, continuity puts the endpoint image in a neighborhood with the first integral $S$ from the hypothesis; hence $D(S\circ F_\alpha)=0$. On a small convex parameter ball, [F3] makes $S\circ F_\alpha$ constant. Choose a closed box with rational endpoints, containing $s$ in its interior and contained in that ball. Its image under $F_\alpha$ is compact by [F6], lies in one level of $S$, and has empty interior in $U$: a nonempty open subset of that image would make $S$ constant on an open set, contradicting $dS=\mu\omega\ne0$. Thus the image is a closed nowhere-dense subset of $U$. By [F5], enumerate the countable collection of all finite words and rational closed parameter boxes; for an admissible box whose compact image has empty interior record that image, and otherwise record the empty set. Include the singleton $\{q\}$ for the empty word. This explicitly defined sequence $(K_j)$ of closed nowhere-dense sets covers $\mathcal O(q)$, since every duration tuple admits the small box just constructed. No countable atlas or choice of first integrals is needed for the enumeration.

Let $V$ be any nonempty open subset of $U$. Choose a rational open Euclidean ball with closure contained in $V$. Recursively choose the first ball in a fixed enumeration of rational balls whose closure is inside the preceding open ball, disjoint from $K_j$, and whose radius is below $2^{-j}$. Such a ball exists because $K_j$ is closed with empty interior. If the $j$th ball has center $c_j$ and radius $r_j<2^{-j}$, then all later centers lie in its closed ball, so $|c_k-c_j|\le r_j$ for $k>j$. Thus the centers form a Cauchy sequence; [F7] gives a limit $p$ in all the nested closed balls, hence in $V$ and outside every $K_j$. Each selection is the least natural-number index satisfying explicit nonempty conditions, so it uses no choice axiom. Since the $K_j$ cover $\mathcal O(q)$, step 2.1 shows $p$ is not horizontally reachable from $q$ even by a path in $U$, and therefore not by one in $V$. This proves the asserted conclusion for every nonempty open $V$, using no global first integral or choice axiom.

case_scope.source_excerpt: Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $E:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable, and let $J\subset\mathbb R$ be open. Suppose $Z(\beta):=\int e^{-\beta E}\,d\mu$ satisfies $0<Z(\beta)<\infty$ on $J$, and for every compact interval $K\subset J$ there is $G_K\in L^1(\mu)$ with $(1+|E|^2)e^{-\beta E}\le G_K$ pointwise for every $\beta\in K$. Define $p_\beta=e^{-\beta E}/Z(\beta)$, $\langle Y\rangle_\beta:=\int Yp_\beta\,d\mu$ for integrable $Y$, and $\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E):=\int(E-\langle E\rangle_\beta)^2p_\beta\,d\mu$. Then $Z\in C^2(J)$, $Z'=-\int E e^{-\beta E}d\mu$, $Z''=\int E^2e^{-\beta E}d\mu$, and $-\partial_\beta\log Z=\langle E\rangle_\beta$, $\partial_\beta^2\log Z=\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E)$. The reference-relative entropy $-\int p_\beta\log p_\beta\,d\mu$ is finite and equals $\log Z+\beta\langle E\rangle_\beta$.

boundaries.evidence: When E=0 and the reference measure is finite positive, the identities reduce to Z=mu(X), mean and variance zero; steps 1.1–3.1 apply.

case_scope.source_excerpt: A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where $[-\infty,\infty]$ has its order topology: finite open intervals and the endpoint neighborhoods $[-\infty,a)$ and $(a,\infty]$ form a basis. Its Borel sigma-algebra is generated by these open sets. A complex-valued function is measurable exactly when its finite real and imaginary parts are measurable, equivalently for the usual Borel structure of $\mathbb C$. Almost-everywhere assertions mean outside a measurable $\mu$-null set; completeness of $\mu$ is not assumed. Nonnegative extended addition uses $a+\infty=\infty+a=\infty$ for $a\in[0,\infty]$; positive scalars multiply $\infty$ to $\infty$, while $0\cdot\infty=0$. Signed expressions $\infty-\infty$ remain undefined and are not used in signed integrals. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where $[-\infty,\infty]$ has its order topology: finite open intervals and the endpoint neighborhoods $[-\infty,a)$ and $(a,\infty]$ form a basis. Its Borel sigma-algebra is generated by these open sets. A complex-valued function is measurable exactly when its finite real and imaginary parts are measurable, equivalently for the usual Borel structure of $\mathbb C$. Almost-everywhere assertions mean outside a measurable $\mu$-null set; completeness of $\mu$ is not assumed. Nonnegative extended addition uses $a+\infty=\infty+a=\infty$ for $a\in[0,\infty]$; positive scalars multiply $\infty$ to $\infty$, while $0\cdot\infty=0$. Signed expressions $\infty-\infty$ remain undefined and are not used in signed integrals. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

citations.quote:
Throughout, $\mathbb F$ is $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and families are indexed by
an arbitrary set $I$, with no enumeration or countability assumed. Finite real lists use [[def-finite-sum]], and sums over finite subsets use [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] in the additive monoid of the scalar field. Disjoint splitting is [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], and scalar modulus estimates use [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]; all suprema and infima of real sets below are
taken in the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) or in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]], [[lem-extended-reals-complete]]).

**Sums of nonnegative families.** Let $(c_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of
nonnegative reals and let $\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ be the set of finite subsets of
$I$, ordered by inclusion. Define

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i:=\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{i\in F}c_i \;:\; F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)\Bigr\}\in[0,+\infty] .$$

The set of finite subsums is nonempty, since $\varnothing$ contributes the empty
sum $0$, so the supremum exists in $[0,+\infty]$; it is a real number exactly
when the finite subsums are bounded above in $\mathbb R$, and $+\infty$
otherwise. For finite $I$ the finite subsum at $I$ is the largest of all finite
subsums, because all terms are nonnegative, so the definition agrees with the
finite sum; in particular $\sum_{i\in I}c_i=0$ when every $c_i$ is $0$, and
$I=\varnothing$ gives the empty sum $0$.

**Splitting identity and small tails.** Fix a finite $F\subseteq I$. Every
finite $G\subseteq I$ splits as the disjoint union $(G\cap F)\cup(G\setminus F)$,
so $\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in G\cap F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i\le\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i$;
conversely the finite $G$ with $F\subseteq G$ satisfy
$\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i$. Taking suprema,
with the constant $\sum_{i\in F}c_i$ passing through the supremum,

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i . \qquad (1)$$

Consequently, if $S:=\sum_{i\in I}c_i$ is finite, then for every real
$\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite $F\subseteq I$ with
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i<\varepsilon$: the finite subsums form a nonempty
bounded-above set with supremum $S$, so by the epsilon characterisation of the
supremum ([[lem-sup-epsilon]]) some finite $F$ has
$S-\varepsilon<\sum_{i\in F}c_i$, and (1) gives
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i=S-\sum_{i\in F}c_i<\varepsilon$. Such an $F$ is
called a **tail-control set** for $\varepsilon$.

**Sums of scalar families.** Now let $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family in $\mathbb F$
and put $s_F:=\sum_{i\in F}a_i$ for finite $F\subseteq I$. The set
$\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ with inclusion is a directed preorder: it is nonempty and
$F\cup G$ is a common upper bound of $F$ and $G$
([[def-directed-set-and-net]]). Hence $(s_F)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$ is a
net in $\mathbb F$, the **finite-subset net** of the family, and the family is
**summable** when this net converges
([[def-net-convergence-and-cluster-point]]). The scalar metric is the usual real metric or [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. These metric spaces are Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]]. A net in $\mathbb F$ has at most one limit
([[thm-hausdorff-iff-net-limits-are-unique]]), so for a summable family the
limit is unique and we write $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\lim_F s_F$ for it. The family is
**absolutely summable** when $\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|<+\infty$ in the sense above.

**Every absolutely summable family is summable, in ZF.** Assume
$S:=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|$ is finite and put $S_F:=\sum_{i\in F}|a_i|$ for finite
$F$. For finite $F,G\subseteq I$ the triangle inequality for finite sums and the
fact that a finite subsum is at most the whole nonnegative sum give

$$|s_F-s_G|\le\sum_{i\in F\triangle G}|a_i|\le S-S_{F\cap G} . \qquad (2)$$

Now fix a real $\varepsilon>0$, let $F_0$ be a tail-control set for
$\varepsilon$, and let $F,G\supseteq F_0$ be finite. Then $F\cap G\supseteq F_0$,
so $S-S_{F\cap G}\le S-S_{F_0}<\varepsilon$ and (2) gives
$|s_F-s_G|<\varepsilon$.

First suppose $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. For each finite $F$ define
$A_F:=\inf\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ and $B_F:=\sup\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ over
finite $G$. Both are real numbers, because $|s_G|\le S_G\le S$, so the two sets
are nonempty and bounded, and $A_F\le B_F$. If $H\supseteq F$ then
$A_H\ge A_F$ and $B_H\le B_F$. Let $L:=\sup_FA_F$ and $U:=\inf_FB_F$.
Since $A_F\le s_{F\cup H}\le B_H$ for all finite $F,H$, we get $L\le U$.
Moreover, the preceding estimate holds for every pair $F,G\supseteq F_0$;
taking the supremum over $F$ and the infimum over $G$ gives
$B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$. Hence
$0\le U-L\le B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so
$L=U=:s$. If $F\supseteq F_0$, then both $s_F$ and $s$ lie in
$[A_{F_0},B_{F_0}]$, and therefore $|s_F-s|\le\varepsilon$.

If $\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, apply the real argument just proved to the families
$(\operatorname{Re}a_i)$ and $(\operatorname{Im}a_i)$. They are absolutely
summable because $|\operatorname{Re}a_i|,|\operatorname{Im}a_i|\le|a_i|$.
Their finite-subset nets converge to real numbers $r$ and $t$, respectively,
so $s_F\to r+it$ in $\mathbb C$. Thus every absolutely summable real or complex
family is summable. **No choice principle is used**: the construction uses only
two-sided suprema in $\mathbb R$.

**Linearity and absolute value.** If $(a_i)$ and $(b_i)$ are absolutely
summable and $\lambda\in\mathbb F$, then so are $(a_i+b_i)$ and
$(\lambda a_i)$, and

$$\sum_{i\in I}(a_i+b_i)=\sum_{i\in I}a_i+\sum_{i\in I}b_i,\qquad \sum_{i\in I}\lambda a_i=\lambda\sum_{i\in I}a_i,\qquad \Bigl|\sum_{i\in I}a_i\Bigr|\le\sum_{i\in I}|a_i| ,$$

because the corresponding identities hold for every finite subsum, both sides
are limits of the corresponding finite-subset nets, and addition, scalar
multiplication and the modulus are continuous. The splitting identity (1)
likewise passes to absolutely summable scalar families:
$\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{i\in F}a_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}a_i$ for every finite
$F$, because finite subsums over sets containing $F$ converge to the left-hand
side and equal the finite sum over $F$ plus the finite subsum of the tail, whose
net converges to the tail sum.

**The finite-dimensional Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.** Let $(u_k)_{0\le k<m}$ and $(v_k)_{0\le k<m}$ be scalar lists, for $m\in\mathbb N$ and let $t\in\mathbb R$. Every term of
$\sum_{k<m}(|u_k|-t|v_k|)^2$ is nonnegative, so for all real $t$

$$0\le\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2-2t\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|+t^2\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2 .$$

If $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2>0$, substituting
$t=\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)/\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$ gives
$\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)^2\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$;
if $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2=0$ then every $v_k=0$ and both sides are $0$. In either case
$\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$
after taking square roots, and applying the modulus inequality for finite sums
to $u_k\overline{v_k}$ also gives

$$\Bigl|\sum_{k<m}u_k\overline{v_k}\Bigr|\le\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2} . \qquad (3)$$

**The space $\ell^2(I)$.** For a family $a=(a_i)_{i\in I}$ in $\mathbb F$ define
$Q(a):=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|^2$. If $Q(a)$ is finite, set $\|a\|_2:=\sqrt{Q(a)}$, using the nonnegative real square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]]; if $Q(a)=+\infty$, set $\|a\|_2:=+\infty$. This is a case definition, not exponentiation of an extended real. Let

$$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F):=\{\,a=(a_i)_{i\in I} : \|a\|_2<+\infty\,\}.$$

The set $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is a vector space over $\mathbb F$: it contains the
zero family, is closed under scalar multiplication because
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$, and is closed under addition because (3)
applied to finite subsums gives $\|a+b\|_2\le\|a\|_2+\|b\|_2<+\infty$. The same
inequality is the triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|_2$, which is moreover
nonnegative, vanishes only for the zero family (an arbitrary sum of nonnegative
terms with supremum $0$ has every term $0$) and satisfies
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$; thus $\|\cdot\|_2$ is a norm on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$. Finally the **pairing**
$\langle a,b\rangle:=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\overline{b_i}$ is well defined on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)\times\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$, because
$|a_i\overline{b_i}|=|a_i||b_i|$ has finite nonnegative sum by (3); it is linear
in the first variable, conjugate symmetric, positive definite, and satisfies
$\langle a,a\rangle=\|a\|_2^2$, all by the corresponding finite identities and
the linearity of the sum. Consequently $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is an inner-product
space, and $e_i\in\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ denotes the family that is $1$ at $i$ and
$0$ elsewhere. **Nothing here asserts that $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is complete**;
that follows later, from an orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space.

reviewed.reason: The F1 assertion defines the norm of one indexed coefficient family and the coordinate pairing of two such vectors. The supplier explicitly allows arbitrary I and states this inner-product structure. Calling the coefficients a family does not generalize the arity of the pairing.

citations.quote: The metric space $\mathbb C$ is complete. A sequence $z_n=x_n+iy_n$ converges to $x+iy$ exactly when $x_n\to x$ and $y_n\to y$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]], [[thm-componentwise-convergence-and-completeness]].

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $I$ be a finite or countably infinite set with a specified enumeration, let $E_i\in\mathbb R$, and let $\ell^2(I):=\{x:I\to\mathbb C:\sum_i|x_i|^2<\infty\}$ with inner product $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_i x_i\overline{y_i}$, linear in the first variable. Write $u_i$ for the coordinate unit vector at $i$. The diagonal multiplication operator $H_E$ is the linear operator with domain $D(H_E):=\{x\in\ell^2(I):\sum_i|E_ix_i|^2<\infty\}$ and action $(H_Ex)_i:=E_ix_i$. [[lem-tdmath-diagonal-model-hilbert-and-domain]] proves completeness of the coefficient space, linearity and density of this domain, and linearity of the coordinate action before the Hilbert-space operator interpretation is used. Its domain is part of the operator data in the sense of [[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]].

derivations.claim: The sequence is norm bounded, say $\|x^{(n)}\|\le M$. For each coordinate, $|x_i^{(n)}-x_i^{(m)}|\le\|x^{(n)}-x^{(m)}\|$, so [F2] gives a unique limit $x_i$. For every finite $F\subset I$, passing to the limit in its finite sum gives $\sum_{i\in F}|x_i|^2\le M^2$. Taking the finite-subset supremum proves $x\in\ell^2(I)$. No selection of nonunique coordinate limits is involved.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $d\ge1$, let $\phi$ be a stable pair
potential as in [[def-tdmath-stable-power-tempered-particle-model]] with
stability constant $B$, and fix $a,\beta>0$. In fixed reference length and
energy units, put $\Lambda_L=[0,L]^d$ and define, for $N\ge1$,
$$Z_{L,N}:=\frac{a^N}{N!}\int_{\Lambda_L^N}e^{-\beta U_N(q_1,\ldots,q_N)}\,d\lambda_d^{\otimes N},$$
where $\lambda_d$ is Lebesgue measure restricted to the Borel subsets of
$\mathbb R^d$, $\lambda_d^{\otimes N}$ is its $N$-fold product measure. The
integrand uses the ordinary real exponential when $U_N<+\infty$ and is defined
to be $0$ when $U_N=+\infty$. Also,
$\int_{\Lambda_L^N}f\,d\lambda_d^{\otimes N}$ abbreviates the nonnegative
integral of $f\mathbf1_{\Lambda_L^N}$ on the full product space, using
[[def-tdmath-measure-integral]]. Set $Z_{L,0}=1$.
Define $\Xi_L:=\sum_{N=0}^{\infty}Z_{L,N}$ as the nonnegative extended sum of
[[def-nonnegative-extended-series]]. For $L\ge1$ put
$Q:=a e^{\beta B}$. Choose any real $K>eQ+1$ and set
$$n_L:=\lfloor K L^d\rfloor+1.$$
which satisfies $K L^d<n_L\le K L^d+1$ by the integer-part lemma
[[lem-integer-part]]. Let
$\Xi_L^{\mathrm{cut}}:=\sum_{N=0}^{n_L}Z_{L,N}$. Then
$$1\le\Xi_L\le e^{Q L^d},\qquad \sum_{N>n_L}Z_{L,N}\le e^{-L^d},\qquad \Xi_L^{\mathrm{cut}}\ge(1-e^{-L^d})\Xi_L.$$
